metadata.title: What is a Wraparound Wrap Note Mortgage-Subject to-Land Contract
metadata.author: kris haskins
metadata.shortDescription:
What is a Wrap Note, Wraparound Mortgages, in real estate along with buying houses Subject To, Land Contracts & All Inclusive Deeds of Trust.  WOW!  If all this sounds confusing, today Real Estate Attorney Bill Bronchick and I will explain & demystify how all this works with creative real estate investing to help you buy or sell your next house.  
     In today's litigious society, us real estate investors must cover our assets when buying houses subject to, so using the Wrap strategy helps us make sure not only we're covered, but the seller's covered as well.  We don't want a judge to think we're taking advantage of grandma & grandpa right?!?!?!   You see, when you buy a house using the traditional Subject To strategy, it leaves the seller with no recourse should you decide or be forced to not make the payment.  But if you create a Wrap note, then the seller has the power to come and foreclose taking back the house if you default.  Today you'll see how that's all set up and further Bill will show us how we sell these houses using a Land Contract so we maintain ownership on title.  

Need Financing?  Find out how much you qualify for in Business Credit Lines: https://www.fundandgrow.com/webinar-registration/krishaskins

Download ALL of Bill's Wrap Note Documents here: https://aw8d9fb.aweb.page/p/ebbaaf8c-c216-4e24-8666-1a85bb7c0716

0:55 - Why judges don't like Subject to
1:39 - What is a wraparound Mortgage or Wraparound Deed of Trust
3:50 - Wraparound mortgage explained
5:55 - Why are wraparound mortgage important
7:52 - Attorney Bill Bronchick explains Wraparound mortgages
10:00 - Difference between a 2nd mortgage and a wraparound mortgage
11:30 - When to use Wraparound mortgages
13:30 - The best houses to use Wrap Notes on
15:30 - Wraparound Addendum
16:18 - All Inclusive Wraparound Promissory Note
17:10 - Wraparound Rider to Deed of Trust and Mortgage
18:18 - Land Contract explained
19:27 - Why don't we BUY houses like we SELL houses

metadata.author: Scott Horne's Owner Finance Network
metadata.shortDescription:
In this week’s video, Scott will go over the details of how a wrap-around mortgage works, what a wrap-around mortgage is, how to structure it, and what type of documents you’ll need to do this type of transaction.

In this video, we’ll be talking about the following:

Intro – 0:00
Assumptions - 0:24
The Documents that are Needed – 1:09
What Is a Wrap-Around Mortgage – 1:56
How to Properly Draft the Documents Needed – 3:30
How to Structure a Wrap-Around Mortgage – 4:25
What Is a Double Wrap Mortgage – 5:21
Loan Servicing – 7:00
Due on Sale Clause – 7:32
Outro – 10:09

Scott Horne has been a real estate, title attorney, and investor for over 30 years. Over this time, he has purchased, rehabbed, and sold over 7,000 single family homes. Through his companies and law office, he has transacted over 10,000 creative finance deals. Scott’s experience as both an attorney and an investor puts him in a unique position to help you navigate this tricky business every step of the way.

What is a wraparound mortgage, how does the money flow, and when should you use a wrap instead of going straight subject‑to? In this video, attorney‑investor Scott Horne breaks down acquisition wraps (including mirror wraps with balloons) and exit wraps when selling to a homeowner, plus the paperwork, disclosures, and servicing best practices that keep you out of trouble.

You’ll learn:
Wrap basics & money flow (borrower → you → underlying lender)
When an acquisition wrap makes sense (e.g., adding a balloon the seller wants)
Using wraps when selling: higher price, higher rate, more exit options
Note sale strategy (why wraps can 3–4× profit vs. a basic flip)
Proper buyer processing (RMLO, reasonable DTI)
The documents you need (wrap note, wrap deed of trust, deed provisions)
Key disclosures (do‑on‑sale, underlying debt, state forms; TX requires English/Spanish)
Loan servicing setup to protect everyone

If this helped, 👍 Like, 💬 Comment, and 🔔 Subscribe for daily creative‑finance training.

03:54 Why wraps: price, rate, repairs, exits
04:31 Note‑sale strategy to 3–4× profit

06:23 Required documents for a wrap
06:59 State disclosures (TX English/Spanish)
07:16 Do‑on‑sale & loan servicing setup
08:01 Title insurance & closing costs
08:27 Wrap‑up & next steps

Scott Horne has been a real estate, title attorney, and investor for over 30 years. Over this time, he has purchased, rehabbed, and sold over 7,000 single family homes. Through his companies and law office, he has transacted over 10,000 creative finance deals. Scott’s experience as both an attorney and an investor puts him in a unique position to help you navigate this tricky business every step of the way.

metadata.title: Subject-To Wraparound: The Creative Finance Cheat Code You’re Not Using (Tampa)
metadata.author: Dom Inglese
metadata.shortDescription:
If you’re an investor, wholesaler, or agent and you’re NOT using subject-to wraparound deals, you’re leaving a literal creative finance cheat code on the table.

In this Tampa case study, I break down exactly how a subject-to wraparound mortgage turns a low-rate bank loan into upfront equity and monthly cashflow using a wraparound seller-financing structure. This is the kind of deal most people walk right past because they don’t understand how the numbers actually work.

Use this as the practical case study, then go watch the full Wrap Strategy Whiteboard training on my channel for the entire framework.

🧠 What You’ll Learn

How a subject-to acquisition sets up a profitable wraparound mortgage

Why low fixed-rate loans in markets like Tampa are gold for creative finance

How to structure resale price, down payment, and new note to create instant equity

How the interest rate spread creates monthly cashflow on a wrap

How amortization and rate differences build back-end equity over time

⏱️ Timestamps / Chapters

0:00 – Creative Finance Whiteboard Intro: Why Subject-To Wraps Matter
Kickoff to the creative finance whiteboard series and why subject-to wraparound mortgages are so powerful in today’s real estate market.

0:28 – CS Wrap Strategy Overview: Tampa Subject-To Wrap Deal Setup
High-level CS Wrap Strategy walkthrough and why this Tampa subject-to wrap case study is the perfect example for investors, wholesalers, and agents.

0:55 – Subject-To Acquisition Explained: Taking Over the Low-Rate Loan
Breaking down how we bought the property subject-to the existing mortgage in Tampa and why a low fixed-rate loan is the foundation of a great wraparound deal.

1:35 – Finding the Wrap Buyer: Creative Finance vs Traditional Bank Loan
How we sourced a buyer who didn’t go the bank route and why a wraparound seller-finance structure beat a traditional conventional loan for this scenario.

2:05 – Wrap Price & Down Payment: Creating Upfront Equity on the Wrap
Step-by-step look at the wrap sale price, the buyer’s down payment, and how that generated instant equity on this subject-to wrap strategy.

2:46 – Interest Rate Spread & New Note Terms: Building Long-Term Equity
Comparing the original subject-to mortgage to the new wrap note, explaining how the interest rate spread and principal balances create equity growth over time.

3:25 – Monthly Cashflow Spread: How the Wraparound Mortgage Prints Cashflow
Showing the monthly payment difference between the underlying loan and the wrap, and how that spread turns into consistent monthly cashflow on this Tampa creative finance deal.

3:58 – Why Subject-To Wraparound Wins in Today’s Rate Environment
Why subject-to wraparound mortgages are such a strong creative finance cheat code when rates are high and buyers still need workable payments.

4:35 – Next Steps: More Wrap Strategy Whiteboards & Creative Finance Training
Closing thoughts and an invite to dive into the full Wrap Strategy Whiteboard and other subject-to / seller finance / wrap trainings on the channel.

🔗 Watch Next: Full Wrap Strategy Whiteboard

This video shows one Tampa subject-to wrap deal.
For the full framework on finding, analyzing, and structuring wraps:

https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=VRUDR8FXNo0

Investors who want real numbers on subject-to wraparound mortgage deals

Wholesalers & bird dogs who keep seeing low-rate loans but don’t know how to monetize them

Agents who want to understand creative finance so they can keep more deals alive

Anyone trying to build cashflow and equity using subject-to, wraps, and seller finance in Tampa Bay and similar markets

metadata.author: Scott Horne's Owner Finance Network
metadata.shortDescription:
Can you buy an existing wraparound mortgage? And can you buy a property subject to both the original first-lien debt and the wrap?

In this video, Scott Horne from Owner Finance Network explains how these layered creative-finance transactions work, including what he informally calls a “Sub 3” or a wrap of a wrap.

Scott covers:

buying and assigning an existing wrap note
controlling the underlying mortgage
authorization forms, powers of attorney, and account access
bank and DSCR debt beneath a wrap
loan servicing and payment allocation
buyer assumptions versus creating a new wrap
processing the new buyer
protecting your future note-sale strategy
due-on-sale and investor-held loan risks
insurance and other details investors must evaluate

The biggest lesson: buying the note is not enough. You need the ability to monitor, manage, and protect every layer beneath it.

Scott Horne has been a real estate, title attorney, and investor for over 30 years. Over this time, he has purchased, rehabbed, and sold over 7,000 single family homes. Through his companies and law office, he has transacted over 10,000 creative finance deals. Scott’s experience as both an attorney and an investor puts him in a unique position to help you navigate this tricky business every step of the way.

metadata.shortDescription:
Inside a Real Wraparound Deal in Seminole Heights, Tampa (Bought Subject-To, Cashflows Like Crazy)

I picked up this block house in Seminole Heights, Tampa subject-to the existing mortgage at a crazy low fixed interest rate — and now I’m turning it into a wraparound mortgage deal that could net close to $1,000/month in nearly passive cash flow.

In this video, I’ll take you inside the property and inside the numbers so you can see exactly how a subject-to + wrap strategy works in a real Tampa neighborhood, step-by-step — not theory.

Here’s what you’ll see inside this Tampa real estate investment property tour:

The deal I took over subject-to:
How we bought this Seminole Heights home subject to the existing low-rate mortgage, what the payment looks like, and why I’m never letting that rate go.

The wraparound strategy explained in plain English:
How I’ll resell this house with seller financing on a wrap at a higher interest rate and become the bank — creating a monthly spread between the underlying loan and the new loan.

Who the “penalty box” buyer is (and why they’re happy to pay more):
ITIN borrowers, self-employed folks, and “non-bankable” buyers who can afford the payment but can’t qualify with traditional financing. I show how this becomes a win-win path to homeownership for them and an amazing deal for us.

Why I loved this specific Seminole Heights property:

Block construction, concrete slab

Metal roof with a long remaining lifespan

Upgraded 200-amp electrical panel

Great neighborhood in Seminole Heights, Tampa
These bones make it ideal for a long-term, low-maintenance creative finance play.

Easy value-add: from 3 bed / 1 bath to true primary suite:
I walk through how converting the laundry room into a second full bath could add tens of thousands in value for a fraction of the cost — and how moving the washer/dryer to the enclosed back porch makes it all work.

Light rehab, big difference:
Simple upgrades — fresh paint, new LVP flooring, new fans and fixtures — totally changed the look of the bedrooms and made the property turnkey for a wrap buyer or a standard renter.

Multiple exit strategies (this is where most investors lose):
I break down several ways I could monetize this Tampa rental property if the wrap buyer doesn’t appear on schedule:

Sell on a wraparound mortgage (Plan A)

Rent it traditionally and still cashflow

Force appreciation by adding the second bath and increasing value
This is how you structure deals so you can be wrong and still be okay.

How I find wrap buyers (hint: agents are your best friends):
I explain how building relationships with buyer’s agents who work with non-traditional borrowers makes you the first call when they have a client who can’t get bank financing — so the agent gets paid, buyer gets a home, and you become the bank.

All of this is part of my personal challenge to hit a specific number of rental/creative finance properties by my next birthday — and this Seminole Heights wrap deal is one of my favorite examples of why creative finance in Tampa still works

If you’re an investor, wholesaler, or agent and you want to:

Learn how to buy properties subject-to low-rate mortgages
Sell them on wraparound mortgages to “penalty box” buyers
Or structure multiple exits so you protect yourself on every deal…

metadata.title: What is a Seller Finance Wrap Around Mortgage | EXPLAINED!
metadata.author: Chris Goff
metadata.shortDescription:
In this training video, you’ll learn what a Seller Finance Wraparound Mortgage is. Along with how it works and when you would use it.

So today, I queried all Absentee Owners in the entire U.S., where the property value is above $300K, with at least 20% equity and they’ve owned the home for at least 2 years. And that number is: 7,284,401. This is mostly single-family residential properties because this is the ideal marketplace to do this.

Now for those of you that are just getting started, when we refer to wraps, we’re talking about seller financing where the owner is willing to basically be the bank and there’s an existing mortgage. 

This is great real estate strategy when you don’t want to apply for a normal bank loan or have it on your credit report.

metadata.title: Wraparound Mortgages Explained How They Work and the Due on Sale Landmine
metadata.author: Tim Talks Real Estate
metadata.shortDescription:
A wraparound mortgage lets a buyer ride on top of the seller's existing low-rate loan and get into a house without qualifying at today's rates — but there's a landmine buried underneath it that can call the whole deal due overnight. In plain English, here's how a wrap actually works, how the money really moves, and the one clause in the seller's original loan that almost nobody selling you on the idea mentions out loud.

In this video:
- What a wraparound mortgage actually is (and how it's a form of seller financing)
- How the money really moves — buyer pays seller, seller pays the original bank
- Why buyers and sellers both love it in a high-rate market
- The due-on-sale clause — the landmine that can call the entire loan due
- Who a wrap actually fits, and how to do it safely
- The one question that protects you before you ever sign

I don't originate loans, so there's nothing being sold to you here — just the honest breakdown.

Run the free affordability calculator: https://timtalksrealestate.com/afford
Creative financing plain-English guide: https://timtalksrealestate.com/creative-financing

Educational only, not financial advice. Program terms change — confirm specifics with a licensed professional.

segments.text: There's a kind of home financing that
lets a buyer basically ride on top of
the seller's existing low rate mortgage,
pay a little more than the old payment,
skip the bank entirely, and get into a
house they couldn't qualify for the
normal way. It sounds almost too clever
to be legal. It's called a wraparound
mortgage, and it's very real, but
there's a landmine buried underneath it
that can blow the whole deal up
overnight. and the people selling you on
the idea almost never mention it. So
today I'll walk you through how a wrap
works and where the trap is before
anybody talks you into one. By the end
of this video you're going to know what
a wraparound mortgage actually is, how
the money really moves, why buyers and
sellers both get excited about it in a
high rate market. and the one clause
sitting in the seller's original loan
that can call the whole thing due with
almost no warning. Stick with me to the
end because the landmine isn't the wrap
itself. It's a single sentence in a loan
document most people never read. So,
let's start with the plain English
version. A wraparound mortgage is a form
of seller financing.
Picture a seller who owns a home and
still has a mortgage on it. Let's say
they locked in a great rate a few years
back. Instead of getting their own brand
new loan from a bank, the buyer and the
seller strike a deal directly. The buyer
pays the seller. The seller keeps their
original mortgage in place and keeps
making those payments to their bank. And
the buyer's new loan from the seller
wraps around that existing loan. That's
where the name comes from. It's a new,
larger loan laid right on top of the old
one that's still underneath. Here's how
the money moves because this is the part
people get fuzzy on. The buyer makes one
monthly payment to the seller, not to a
bank, based on the full wraparound loan,
usually at a rate a bit higher than the
seller's old rate. The seller takes that
money, keeps paying the original
mortgage to the original lender, just
like always, and pockets the difference.
So, the seller earns a little spread
every month. The buyer gets into the
home without qualifying at today's
rates, and the underlying loan just
keeps humming along in the background.
In most cases, the bank underneath
doesn't even know the house changed
hands. Now, you can see why both sides
get excited, especially when rates are
high. Imagine an old loan at 3% while
new loans are up near 7%. The buyer gets
a payment tied to a cheaper old loan
instead of an expensive new one. The
seller sells a house that might
otherwise sit and earns interest on top.
A buyer who can't get a traditional
approval suddenly has a path. On paper,
everybody wins. So, here's the landmine,
and I want you completely cleareyed on
it. Almost every regular mortgage in
this country contains something called a
do on sale clause. That clause says if
you sell or transfer the property, the
lender has the right to demand the
entire loan balance back immediately.
Not the monthly payment, the whole thing
all at once. And a wraparound almost

metadata.title: Risks and Considerations of Wraparound and Subject-To Financing Offers
metadata.author: Bramlett Partners Real Estate
metadata.shortDescription:
This conversation discusses the topics of wraparound offers and subject-to offers in real estate. It explains the differences between the two types of offers and why sellers are receiving them. The conversation also explores the risks and considerations involved in accepting these offers, such as the due-on-sale clause and the potential impact on credit. It provides guidance on how to handle these offers as an agent or seller, including evaluating the down payment, credit, and interest rate. Overall, the conversation aims to inform listeners about wraparound and subject-to offers and help them make informed decisions.

-- Wraparound offers involve transferring title to the buyer while keeping the existing mortgage, while subject-to offers involve transferring both title and mortgage to the buyer.
-- Sellers are receiving these offers due to the difference in mortgage rates between when they purchased the property and the current market rates.
-- Accepting wraparound or subject-to offers carries risks, such as the due-on-sale clause and potential impact on credit.
-- Considerations when evaluating these offers include the down payment, buyer's credit, and interest rate.
-- Involving an attorney is crucial when dealing with wraparound or subject-to offers.

metadata.title: Don't Get Burned by Wrap-Around Mortgages and Subject-to Financing!
metadata.author: Straight Up Mortgage Talk
metadata.shortDescription:
A wrap around mortgage is a type of financing where the seller of a property agrees to finance the sale themselves, essentially acting as a bank for the buyer. While this can be an attractive option for buyers who may not qualify for traditional financing, it also comes with risks.

One of the biggest risks of a wrap around mortgage is the possibility of default. If the buyer defaults on the wrap around mortgage, the seller could potentially lose their property, as the wrap around mortgage is typically secured by the property itself.

Additionally, if the original mortgage on the property has a "due on sale" clause, the seller could be at risk of defaulting on their own mortgage if they transfer ownership to the buyer through a wrap around mortgage.

Wrap around mortgages can be a risky form of financing that require careful consideration and understanding of the potential consequences. It's important for both buyers and sellers to carefully review the terms of the agreement and consult with a professional, such as a real estate attorney or financial advisor, before entering into a wrap around mortgage agreement.

What is a Wraparound Mortgage?

A wraparound mortgage, also known as a "wrap", is a type of secondary financing for the purchase of real property. With a wraparound mortgage, the seller gives the buyer a junior mortgage that “wraps around” an existing mortgage already secured by the property.  Learn more in this short animated video.

metadata.title: How To Use Seller Finance In Real Estate Deals
metadata.author: Pace Morby
metadata.shortDescription:
What is the difference between seller finance and subject to, and why is seller finance actually more difficult to negotiate? In part two of our creative finance series, Pace Morby breaks down exactly how to structure seller finance deals when the seller has no underlying debt. Learn the crucial differences between title and deed, how to protect the seller by ensuring you make money on the deal, and why a slow 1031 exchange is better than a traditional one. Pace also shares multiple real-world examples, including how he bought an RV park for $5 million with zero down, and how to use strategies like a "dating contract" to build trust with hesitant sellers.

metadata.author: Pace Morby
metadata.shortDescription:
Want to buy a cash-flowing business without using your own money? Pace travels to Alaska to break down how SubTo member Carlie Romer used creative finance to buy a carpet cleaning business that nets $25,000 a month for zero money out of pocket. After the business sat on the market for over a year at $400,000, Carly bypassed the broker, negotiated directly with the seller, and secured it for $100,000 on seller finance. metadata.title: What to Say to Sellers on the Phone | Pitching Creative Finance
metadata.author: Pace Morby
metadata.shortDescription:
In the third part of this series, Pace Morby explains creative finance LIVE over the phone with Robbie, the seller on this tricky deal. Watch as he pitches subject to and seller finance to the seller, breaking down why creative finance is the best solution for the seller, agent, and everyone else involved. Not only that, but Pace also lists off the potential drawbacks if the seller were to choose subject to/seller finance. After the call, Pace dives into the specific points he made on the call, describing that it’s quality conversations that convince sellers and agents that going the creative route is always the best option.

Creative finance dominates cash transactions. The faster sellers and agents learn this, the easier real estate transactions will become. Pace also talks about the six reasons why we buy real estate. Throughout this, Pace calculates the numbers on the seller’s deal, explaining why each reason works together. This video is excellent study material for anyone working towards building their seller rapport.

metadata.title: How to Properly Structure Creative Finance Deals
metadata.author: Pace Morby
metadata.shortDescription:
A lot of investors hear “creative finance” and think it means free money. That’s exactly where people get into trouble.

This Dallas stop of the Creative Nation Tour was a make-up event after the original January meetup had to be postponed because of the major ice and snow storm earlier this year.

Pace Morby breaks down why some creative finance deals become dangerous when there’s no real cash flow behind them, the hidden risk of taking huge payouts upfront, and why some no-money-down deals eventually collapse.

The room also turned into a live collaboration session, with investors networking, raising private money, looking for JV partners, and discussing luxury homes, land deals, and co-living opportunities.

One of the biggest takeaways from Dallas: hype might get attention… but sustainable deals win long term.

metadata.title: Determining if a Creative Finance Deal Is Good or Not
metadata.author: Pace Morby
metadata.shortDescription:
What do “terms” mean in a creative finance deal? In today’s video, Pace Morby dives into what terms are in a creative real estate transaction. He walks through a subject to deal he bought from Armando, a community member, explaining what each number - or term - means and how it impacts both him and the seller. 

As he’s discussing the deal, Pace discovers the deal doesn’t cash flow. He renegotiates certain terms, such as the assignment fee, to be more beneficial to him since he know it will take longer for the property to profit. He provides helpful tips to keep in mind when determining if a creative finance deal is a good deal or not. You should be informed of what each term means so you know the correct questions to ask. This video is great to watch if another investor or agent reaches out to you, as the seller, asking if you’d sell your house on terms.

metadata.author: Pace Morby
metadata.shortDescription:
SubTo and Creative Finance are transforming the way real estate agents close deals - especially in markets where traditional listings fall short. In this powerful session, you’ll learn how to use Subject To strategies and Creative Finance methods to close more listings, attract investors, and provide your clients with smarter, faster options.

Discover why so many deals go off-market, how to present creative offers without lowering price, and why agents who master SubTo and Creative Finance stand out from the rest. This isn’t theory—it’s what works in today’s shifting market.

🔑 Topics Covered:

- SubTo and Creative Finance breakdowns
- Agent-investor collaboration tips
- How to secure full-price offers creatively
- Lease options, wraps, and hybrid deals
- Real-world scripts and scenarios from top closers

Perfect for real estate professionals ready to level up with smart, ethical deal structures.

metadata.title: SAFE Act & Dodd‑Frank for Seller Financing: RMLO, RESPA & ATR Explained
metadata.author: Scott Horne's Owner Finance Network
metadata.shortDescription:
If you sell houses with owner financing, compliance isn’t optional. In this quick guide, Scott breaks down how the SAFE Act and Dodd‑Frank impact creative deals with owner‑occupant buyers—when you must use an RMLO, why RESPA disclosures matter, and how ATR (Ability‑to‑Repay) affects your terms. Do this right and you’ll protect yourself and make your notes more marketable in the secondary market.

What you’ll learn
When the SAFE Act applies (and when it doesn’t)
The role of an RMLO and required RESPA docs
ATR/Dodd‑Frank essentials (and why income matters more than credit)
Texas’s “three‑property de minimis” nuance—and why you should process everyone anyway

Compliance tips that help you sell notes for more

This video is for education only and not legal advice. Consult a qualified real estate attorney in your state.

Chapters
00:00 Intro: Why compliance matters
00:16 SAFE Act vs. Dodd‑Frank (big picture)
00:24 What this video covers
00:38 Owner‑occupant focus: when rules kick in
01:12 Two pillars: attorney + RMLO/RESPA
01:37 Most investors miss RESPA—how to fix it
01:57 ATR (Ability‑to‑Repay) under Dodd‑Frank
02:23 Texas “3‑deal” de minimis rule
02:39 Why we still process every buyer
03:04 What RMLO packaging gives you
03:35 APR & other Dodd‑Frank checks
03:59 If a seller asks you to process
04:19 Note sales: why compliance boosts price
04:46 Best practices & takeaways
05:05 Wrap‑up & next steps

Scott Horne has been a real estate, title attorney, and investor for over 30 years. Over this time, he has purchased, rehabbed, and sold over 7,000 single family homes. Through his companies and law office, he has transacted over 10,000 creative finance deals. Scott’s experience as both an attorney and an investor puts him in a unique position to help you navigate this tricky business every step of the way.

metadata.title: Federal Mortgage Laws Explained: RESPA, TILA, ECOA & the SAFE Act
metadata.author: Ameritrain Mortgage Institute
metadata.shortDescription:
Understanding federal mortgage laws is required to become a licensed Mortgage Loan Originator (MLO).

In this video, we break down the four major federal laws every MLO must know for licensing, compliance, and the SAFE exam:

✔️ RESPA (Real Estate Settlement Procedures Act)
✔️ TILA (Truth in Lending Act)
✔️ ECOA (Equal Credit Opportunity Act)
✔️ SAFE Act (Secure and Fair Enforcement for Mortgage Licensing Act)

We explain what each law does, why it exists, and how it impacts mortgage loan originators in real-world lending situations — not just on the exam.

📚 This video is part of our NMLS Pre-License Education series from Ameritrain Mortgage Institute, an NMLS-approved education provider.

👉 Next Step: Continue with our Ethics & Consumer Protection overview.

segments.text: All right. If you're a mortgage loan
originator, you know the regulatory
world can feel well, like a total maze.
So, today we're handing you the map.
We're going to break down the key
federal mortgage laws you absolutely
have to know, but in a way that's clear,
practical, and actually helps you in
your day-to-day. Let's jump in. So,
let's start with the big question,
right? Why on earth are there so many
rules for just one loan? The answer is
pretty simple. A mortgage isn't just any
loan. It's one of the biggest, most
important financial steps a person will
ever take. And with that comes some
serious risk. Every single law we're
about to talk about was built to tackle
a specific risk and to wrap a protective
shield around the borrower. Okay, so how
are we going to tackle all this? Well,
we've organized everything into three
core pillars. Transparency, fair
lending, and what we're calling targeted
safeguards. We'll kick off with the big
picture, dig into each pillar, and then,
and this is the most important part,
we'll tie it all back to your role in
this whole process. So, let's lay the
foundation. You know, if you walk away
with just one thing today, I want it to
be this. Every single rule, every form,
every piece of red tape has the exact
same goal at its heart. Protecting the
borrower. And there it is. This is the
mission statement. This is the why
behind everything else. It's not about
making your job harder. It's about
making sure the market is fair and clear
for everyone trying to buy a home. Keep
this in mind as we go. All right, on to
our first pillar, transparency and
disclosure. I like to think of these as
the sunlight laws. Their whole job is to
shine upright light on the process to
give borrowers clear, upfront info so
they know exactly what they're getting
into. No mystery, no confusion. First
up, we've got RESPA. You can just call
this the no surprises at the closing
table act. It's all about making sure
borrowers see every settlement cost
upfront. But just as importantly, it
completely outlaws kickbacks. That means
no more shady deals where someone gets a
secret feed just for sending business
their way because that stuff just
inflates costs for the consumer. And
then there's Tilla, the Truth in Lending
Act. So if RESPA is about settlement
costs, Tilla is all about the cost of
the money itself. This is the law that
gives us the APR, the annual percentage
rate. It's the magic number that lets a
borrower actually compare different
loans apples to apples to see which one
is the better deal. Now, for a long,
long time, having these two different
laws meant borrowers got a pile of
different forms. You had RESPA
disclosures, you had Tilla disclosures.
It was frankly a mess. super confusing
and just made it hard for people to
figure out what was going on. It was
obvious something had to change. And
that change was TRID. The Consumer
Financial Protection Bureau stepped in
and basically said, "Let's fix this."
They merged those confusing RESPA and
Tilla forms into the two documents you
live and breathe every day. The loan
estimate and the closing disclosure.
Honestly, this was a total game changer
for borrowers. And to round out this
transparency pillar, we have the
Homeowners Protection Act. This law is
all about making sure people don't pay
for private mortgage insurance, you
know, PMI, for a single day longer than
they have to. It sets up clear rules for
when PMI has to be automatically
canceled, which is another huge win for
cost transparency. Okay, let's move on
to our second pillar, and this one is
massive. It's the absolute bedrock of
ethical lending, ensuring a fair shot
for everyone. These laws are designed to
create a level playing field, making
sure every qualified applicant has the
same opportunity to get a loan. The two
heavy hitters here are the Equal Credit
Opportunity Act or EO A and the Fair
Housing Act, the FHA. Think of them as a
power duo working together to flat out
forbid discrimination in housing and
lending. And they do this by defining
what we call protected classes. What
this means is it is illegal to make any
part of a lending decision based on
these things. The only thing that should
matter, the only thing you can focus on
is the applicant's financial picture and
their ability to repay the loan. Period.
So, how do we make sure everybody's
actually following these rules? Well,
that's where HMDA comes in. Think of
HMDA as the accountability engine. It
forces lenders to report data on who's
applying and who's getting loans. This
allows regulators and even the public to
look at the data and spot any patterns
that might suggest discrimination is
happening. It keeps everyone honest. All
right, on to our third and final pillar,
targeted consumer safeguards. Now, if
the first two pillars were about broad
principles, this one zooms in. These
laws are designed to deal with very
specific risks, often protecting
borrowers who might be more vulnerable
or dealing with higher risk loan pipes.
A perfect example is HOPA. This law is
like a special shield for people getting
what are called highcost mortgages. You
know, loans with really high interest
rates or fees. It triggers extra
disclosures, requires counseling, and
puts a stop to risky loan features like
balloon payments that have been used in
predatory lending in the past. And of
course, we can't talk about mortgage
laws without talking about the big one,
the DoddFrank Act. This legislation
completely reshaped the industry after
the 2008 crisis. Now, it's a huge law.
But for you as an MLO, you can really
boil its impact down to three major
things. It created the CFPB. It gave us
the allimportant ability to repay rule.
And it beefed up protections for
homeowners after they've closed on the
loan. So, we have covered a ton of
ground. We've talked about the
landscape, the three pillars of
protection. But now, let's bring it all
home. What does this all actually mean
for you sitting at your desk talking to
clients? And this is really the key
takeaway. You're not just a loan
originator. You're the frontline
guardian of all these protections we've
been talking about. Your knowledge, your
ethics, your commitment. That's what
turns all this legal jargon into a real
tangible safeguard for your clients. At
the end of the day, compliance isn't
just about following rules to avoid
trouble. It's about building trust. It's
about making the dream of home ownership
a little bit safer and a little bit
fairer for everyone you work with. So,
the real question I want to leave you
with is this. How are you going to take
this knowledge and actively champion
these protections for your clients
starting with your very next loan?
[music]

segments.text: The Dodd Frank Wall Street reform and
consumer protection act is legislation
that was passed by the US Congress in
response to financial industry behavior
that led to the financial crisis of 2007
and 2008 it sought to make the US
Financial system safer for consumers and
taxpayers commonly known as the dodf
Frank act or dodf Frank it established a
number of new government agencies tested
with overseeing the various components
of the law and by extension various
aspects of the financial system the
20072 2008 financial crisis is perhaps
the worst economic catastrophe to befall
the country and the world since the Wall
Street crash in 1929 broadly speaking it
was caused by the greed driven behavior
and lacks oversight of financial
institutions the loosening of financial
industry regulations in the decades
leading up to 2007 allowed various types
of institutions in the US Financial
Services industry to lend money in ways
that were riskier than ever before the
housing sector in particular experienced
massive growth that couldn't be
supported the bubble burst sending the
banking industry and Global stock
markets into a downfall it created the
worst Global recession in Generations
Dodd Frank was created to keep anything
similar from ever happening again the
mission or objective of the dod Frank
Act is to promote the financial
stability of the US by improving
accountability and transparency y in the
financial system and to end too big to
fail to protect the American taxpayer by
ending bailouts to protect consumers
from Abus of financial service practices
and also for some other purposes One Way
dodf Frank Works to achieve its mission
is by establishing the Consumer
Financial Protection Bureau which we
know as a
cfpb title 10 establishes within the fed
the cfpb which is tasked with um
regulating Consumer Financial products
and services in compliance with with
federal law the bureau is headed by a
director who is appointed by the
president with the advice and consent of
the senate for a term of 5 years the
bureau is subject to a financial audit
by the government accounting office and
must report to the Senate Banking
Committee and the house Financial
Services committee by anually the
financial stability oversight Council
May issue a stay to the bureau with an
appealable 23s vote even though the
bureau is placed within the FED it
operates independently the FED is
prohibited from interfering with matters
before the director directing any
employee of the bureau modifying the
functions and responsibilities of the
bureau or impeding an order of the
bureau the bureau is separated into six
separate units the Chief Operating
Officer excuse me the Chief Operating
Officer the consumer education
engagement research markets and
regulations supervision enforcement Fair
lending and equal uh opportunity general
counsel and then finally external
Affairs within the the bureau a new
consumer Advisory Board assists the
bureau and informs it of emerging market
trends this board is appointed by the
director of The Bureau with at least six
members recommended by a Regional
Federal Reserve
presidents the bureau may take any
action including prescribing rules to
prevent a covered person this includes
Banks to varying degrees or a service
provider from committing or engaging in
in an unfair deceptive or abusive act or
practice under federal law in connection
with any transaction with a consumer or
a consumer financial product or service
or the offering of a consumer financial
product or
service Additionally the bureau May
prescribe rules as necessary to ensure
that the features of any Consumer
Financial product or service service
both initially and over the term of the
product or service are fully accurately
and effectively effectively disclosed to
consumers in a manner that permits the
consumer to understand the cost benefits
and risks associated with the product or

segments.text: Consumers have raised concerns about the
compensation structure of MLOs, arguing
that it creates a disincentive for them
to offer the best market interest rates.
This compensation process can exacerbate
unfair and predatory practices.
To address these issues, it is crucial
to have a consistent definition of
unfair practices or treatment.
The consistent definition of unfairness
is found in the Federal Trade Commission
Act.
Congress has adopted the standard
developed by the Federal Trade
Commission to determine whether acts or
practices are unfair under Section 5A of
the FTC Act.
According to the FTC Act, an act or
practice is considered unfair if it
causes substantial injury to consumers,
which cannot be reasonably avoided by by
the consumers themselves, and is not
outweighed by countervailing benefits to
consumers or competition.
The FTC may also consider established
public policies in determining
unfairness, but public policy alone
cannot be the primary basis for such a
determination.
The focus of any unfairness inquiry is
consumer injury, which can be
substantial if it affects a large number
of consumers or poses a significant risk
of concrete harm.
States have also enacted statutes that
prohibit unfair or deceptive acts or
practices.
These statutes often define unfairness
as conduct that is considered immoral,
unethical, oppressive, or unscrupulous,
causing substantial injury to consumers.
Based on these definitions, the board
has determined that paying loan
originators based on loan terms or
conditions other than the amount of
credit extended, or steering consumers
towards loans that are not in their best
interest to maximize loan originator
compensation, are unfair practices.
Now, let's summarize the final rule
aimed at protecting consumers in the
mortgage market.
The goal of the amendment is to protect
consumers in the mortgage market from
unfair practices involving compensation
paid to loan originators.
One of the ways this is achieved was the
prohibition on compensation based on
terms or conditions.
Creditors or any other person are
prohibited from paying compensation
compensation to mortgage broker, excuse
me, to mortgage brokers or other loan
originators based on the terms or
conditions of a mortgage transaction
except for the amount of credit
extended.
The rule also put a prohibition on
consumer paid compensation.
No person can pay compensation to a loan
originator for a specific transaction if
the consumer directly pays the loan
originator's compensation.
The rule The rule also put a prohibition
on steering.
Loan originators are prohibited from
directing consumers to loans that
provide that provide greater
compensation to the loan originator
unless the loan is in the consumer's
best interest.
Additionally, the rule provides a safe
harbor for compliance. A safe harbor is
provided to facilitate compliance with
the anti-steering prohibition.
Loan originators are deemed to comply if
they present loan options that offer the
lowest interest rate, no risky features,
and the lowest total dollar amount for
origination points or fees and discount
points.
Finally, let's consider the rule's scope
and coverage.
The rule applies to loan originators
including mortgage brokers and employees
of creditors originating loans.
It covers all transactions secured by a
dwelling but excludes HELOCs under
open-end credit plans and timeshare
transactions.

According to the FTC Act, an act or practice is considered unfair if it causes substantial injury to consumers, which cannot be reasonably avoided by by the consumers themselves, and is not outweighed by countervailing benefits to consumers or competition. The FTC may also consider established public policies in determining unfairness, but public policy alone cannot be the primary basis for such a determination. The focus of any unfairness inquiry is consumer injury, which can be substantial if it affects a large number of consumers or poses a significant risk of concrete harm. States have also enacted statutes that prohibit unfair or deceptive acts or practices. These statutes often define unfairness as conduct that is considered immoral, unethical, oppressive, or unscrupulous, causing substantial injury to consumers. Based on these definitions, the board has determined that paying loan originators based on loan terms or conditions other than the amount of credit extended, or steering consumers towards loans that are not in their best interest to maximize loan originator compensation, are unfair practices. Now, let's summarize the final rule aimed at protecting consumers in the mortgage market. The goal of the amendment is to protect consumers in the mortgage market from unfair practices involving compensation paid to loan originators. One of the ways this is achieved was the prohibition on compensation based on terms or conditions. Creditors or any other person are prohibited from paying compensation compensation to mortgage broker, excuse me, to mortgage brokers or other loan originators based on the terms or conditions of a mortgage transaction except for the amount of credit extended. The rule also put a prohibition on consumer paid compensation. No person can pay compensation to a loan originator for a specific transaction if the consumer directly pays the loan originator's compensation. The rule The rule also put a prohibition on steering. Additionally, the rule provides a safe harbor for compliance. A safe harbor is provided to facilitate compliance with the anti-steering prohibition. Loan originators are deemed to comply if they present loan options that offer the lowest interest rate, no risky features, and the lowest total dollar amount for origination points or fees and discount points. Finally, let's consider the rule's scope and coverage. The rule applies to loan originators including mortgage brokers and employees of creditors originating loans. What is the due-on-sale clause, and how can you avoid it? In this video, I will discuss the due-on-sale clause in real estate. I'll be going over the basics of the clause and how to avoid it so that you can protect your assets and enforce your rights as an investor!

segments.text: Due on sale clauses are a crucial aspect
of mortgage agreements that many
homeowners and potential buyers need to
understand. These clauses require the
full repayment of a mortgage loan when a
property is sold or transferred. But
what exactly does this mean for you? The
due on sale clause, sometimes called an
acceleration clause, gives lenders the
right to demand full payment of the
remaining mortgage balance when a
property changes hands. This protects
lenders from being stuck with below
market interest rates when property
ownership changes. While these clauses
are common, there are important
exceptions. The Garner Act of 1982
established several situations where
lenders cannot enforce a do on sale
clause. These include transfers due to
the borrower's death, transfers between
spouses or to children, and transfers
resulting from divorce or separation
agreements. Assumable mortgages offer
another way to potentially bypass a do
on sale clause. These allow a buyer to
take over the seller's existing mortgage
under the same terms. Governmentbacked
loans like FHA and VA mortgages are
often assumable, but conventional loans
typically are not. Some homeowners
explore using living trusts or land
trusts as a way to transfer property
without triggering the do on sale
clause. While these methods can be
effective for estate planning, using
them solely to avoid the clause carries
risks. Speaking of risks, violating a
due on sale clause can have serious
consequences. If a lender discovers an
unauthorized transfer, they may demand
immediate full repayment of the loan or
even initiate foreclosure
proceedings. However, there are legal
strategies for navigating due on sale
clauses. These include seeking lender
approval for transfers using family
transfer exceptions, negotiating with
the lender, or refinancing before a
planned transfer. Understanding due on
sale clauses is essential for anyone
involved in real estate transactions.
While these clauses can present
challenges, knowing the exceptions and
potential workarounds can help you make
informed decisions about property
transfers. Remember, when dealing with
complex mortgage issues, it's always
wise to consult with a qualified real
estate attorney or financial adviser.

metadata.title: Building Wealth through Non-Performing Mortgage Note Investing
metadata.author: Preferred Trust
metadata.shortDescription:
Lauren Wells, co-founder of 7E Investments, discusses the opportunity for passive income through investing in non-performing mortgage notes secured by single-family homes. She explains how they fix and flip these mortgage notes, turning them into performing assets. Lauren emphasizes the importance of understanding the asset class and the sponsor when considering investments. She also highlights the accessibility of their investment options, including a Reg-A offering with a minimum investment of $5,000. The vision for 7E Investments is to impact over a thousand investors and continue to provide opportunities for people to get in the game.

segments.text: - Hey guys, this is Toby Mathis,
and I'm joined today by Bill Mencarow
who is the only guy I talk to about notes.
He runs a investment group,
which is an educational group and a great platform
that deals with this area.
And today all we're going to talk about
is building wealth with note investing.
It's one area of investing
that a lot of people don't know anything about.
And so we're going to make sure you know about it.
So first off, Bill, thank you for being here.
- Thank you, Toby.
- Yeah, and second off,
what is note investing and why should somebody consider it?
- Well, it's about the only investment I know of
where you can decide what interest rate
you would like on your money.
- That's interesting.
That's a good way to put it.
- (chuckles) And it's a secured investment
unlike a lot of other investments.
So what is it?
Real estate note, people call 'em trust deeds,
mortgages, contracts for deed in some states.
It's a legal document created
when somebody sells a property
and lets the buyer purchase it
without involving conventional lenders.
Instead, very briefly, the buyer pays the property seller
in installment payments over time
for the amount of the purchase price plus interest
less any down payment that was made.
Just to give you a simple example,
let's take a $300,000 single family house.
Somebody is selling their home.
And buyer comes, and it's free and clear,
or it's got a fairly low balance
that can be paid off on the mortgage.
So $300,000 house.
Buyer comes along, gives a 20% down payment, $60,000.
Balance is $240,000.
Now normally they would go to a bank
or some other lender and get that cash.
Well, in this case, the seller of the property says,
no, I will take back a note.
It'll be 9% interest, 15 years,
and the property buyer will then pay the seller
instead of the bank.
Pays the seller every month
in this case about $2,400 a month.
And the note is held by the property seller,
and it's secured by a lien on the property.
So if there's any defaults or anything,
ultimately the seller could get the house back.
And that's in a nutshell what a real estate note is.
- And so somebody's...
So, for example, when you're teaching
and you're teaching people how to invest in notes,
they might go and buy that note from that owner,
or that owner may say, "Hey, you know what?
"I want some more cash.
"I'd like the cash in my pocket."
And they'll go sell that note
similar to what the banks do.
I mean, the banks sell all their mortgages too.
They securitize 'em, right?
So this is just private transaction.
And is that accurate?
Is that what they're doing?
- Oh yeah, it's a negotiable instrument.
You know, the person who takes back the note
when they sell their home and getting $2,400 a month
might someday decide, well, you know, I need more cash
for whatever reason, or I'd like to take a trip
around the world, or whatever it might be.
They'd like a lump sum of cash.
So this note is a negotiable instrument,
and they can sell it to someone else and get cash for it.
They sell it at a discount
because, number one, a lot of the payments
have already been made and, you know, they might have
to sell it at a different interest rate or something.
But no, that's certainly done.
The notes, I should say some may say,
"Oh, 9% that's high for these days."
Although we are getting close to that,
it's for conventional interest rates.
But the seller carryback notes, private notes,
whatever you want to call 'em, usually, quite often,
almost all the time, carry a higher interest rate
than a conventional loan.
And the pros for the seller of the property
who carries back this note,
they can get full price for their property
or even more sometimes.
You know, there's an old saying in real estate.
You can have price or you could have terms,
but you can't have both.
You'll get a higher return.
The property seller can get a higher return
compared to other invest investments, higher interest rate.
There's no waiting or wondering
if the buyer is going to qualify for a conventional loan.
You're quicker closing,
getting a substantial monthly income,
secured by the house that if it's your home,
you know that house and you know how valuable it is,
and it's secured by that house that you might,
God forbid, but if there's a default, you get it back.
And as you alluded to, most people don't know
that you can sell that note,
or you can borrow against it from a bank.
You can sell part of it.
You can sell the next x number of payments,
or you can sell half the note.
You know, you can do all sorts of things with it.
You can trade it.
You could trade it for real estate,
for a down payment on some real estate
or a car or, you know, whatever.
As I say, to use a legal term, it's a negotiable instrument.
And there's a lot more you can do with notes.
It's a tremendously flexible thing.
If we have time, we'll go into one or two of those things.
- No, that's perfect because I think you laid it out.
Now a carryback, like if I'm the owner
and I'm selling a property,
I'm carrying back and I'm holding a piece of paper
that's going to give me an income stream,
I'm doing that because it's spreading the tax hit out.
I can elect to treat it as an installment sale
under 453 and spread it out over many years,
which means I don't have to pay tax
on that sale all in one shot
like if I sold it and there was bank financing.
Here I actually have this thing.
And I've done this, by the way,
actually on behalf of clients that had carryback notes.
What's the typical discount on that?
So let's say that I have $100,000 note
that's getting $2,000 a month.
I don't know, let's just say it's 9% interest.
I don't know if the numbers actually work,
but let's just say you had that note.
Would I sell that to somebody,
and if so, at what discount
is the market usually going to give?
- It depends, of course, on, again,
the investor wants to determine what interest rate
they're going to get on their investment.
So if it's let's say a $100,000 note,
you know, depending on how many payments have been made,
but let's say you know, only a couple payments,
so it's still bounce of $100,000.
You'll probably get somewhere...
It depends of course, on the interest rate.
You said a 9% note.
There wouldn't be a whole lot of discount on that.
There are investors out there who are looking
to buy a note on the secondary market, if you will,
not a second note, but, you know, on a reselling of a note.
Maybe 85,000 you might end up with
because the way it works, as you, Toby, know very well,
but notes are sold at a discount.
And so here, give me example.
I wrote down some numbers here.
This $300,000 house that I mentioned before, $60,000 down,
$240,000 balance, written at 15 years,
about 2,400 bucks a month that the payer is paying.
So the seller wants to sell that note,
and the interest rate that the investor wants is 12%.
Well, you plug that into a financial calculator.
That comes to $200,000.
So the investor pays 200,000 for that note.
Getting $2,400 a month, if you plug that in the calculator,
that's a 12% return on your money.
So, the investor who buys that note
has converted a 9% note to a 12% interest rate note,
yet the terms, the note payer's interest rate, still 9%.
The monthly payment's still the same.
The number of payments doesn't change.
Nothing changes for the note payer itself.
It's just by buying the note at a discount,
you increase your return on your money
from 9% in this case to 12%.
It's not usury
because the payer is not paying anything more.
Payer may not not even know the note has been sold
until he gets a notice,
so we'll make your payments to Mr. Smith now
instead of Mr. Jones.
So it's a kind of a beautiful thing.
And as I say, there's so much.
What I like about it, there's so much you can do
when you own a note, and that's just one example.
- Where do you find them?
So if I'm an investor, that sounds really attractive to me
'cause like I'm looking at it going, hey, right now,
hey, money market might get you 5%,
some CDs gets you 5%.
But you're saying, hey,
I'm willing to take a little more risk.
And I know the market's going nuts right now
with the raising of the interest rates.
Are there any of these out there?
And if so, where do I find them?
- Oh, there are a lot of 'em out there,
and there are a lot more being created now.
You know, it's common sense

fewer people can qualify to get a loan.
Every time we have an uptick in interest rates,
there's a smaller and smaller pool
of potential property buyers.
So when a property seller realizes, hey, you know,
a year or so ago I could have sold this house like that,
but now it's sitting on the market, what do I do?
Well, people can't qualify for a loan,
but maybe I'll offer to hold a note
and in other words be the bank.
Won't be a bank involved.
It'll just be me selling the property
and holding that note and getting the monthly income.
And once you offer what they call seller financing,
again, a word I don't like to use
'cause regulators love the word financing.
It's not financing in my opinion.
Anyway, when you have a seller carryback situation,
properties sell a lot faster,
and they can sell for full price
'cause again, you get terms or you get price,
but you don't get both.
But you asked where to find 'em.
- [Toby] Yeah.
- Well, on our website, we have a link

and we have close to 6,000 members of our Facebook group.

real estate brokers, bank trust officers,
financial planners, cultivate relationships with them.
Let 'em know that you buy notes.

these are the ones you consider.
What's an easy rule to follow for somebody

in note investing?

I would get yourself a mentor

Maybe it's a friend of yours.
Maybe it's, you know...
We'll be happy to help you at no charge.
You know, just send me an email,

but I'm happy to give you some advice.
Specifically for somebody starting out,
I would only stick with first position notes.
I wouldn't go to seconds

I'd look for the type of property.
I would stick with single family houses
unless you really know that you can handle...
I mean, the way I look at it

So, you know, what am I going to do with a factory?
I don't know anything about factories.
So I don't buy notes on factories or shopping centers.
I buy notes on single family houses, on farmland,
you know, some things that I personally know what to do with

So think about that.
Think about the down payment.
What was the down payment that was made?
If it's less than 15 or 20%,

and you might find yourself underwater.
You don't want the property back.
So, the higher the down payment, the better.
Notes that have property that, you know,
you'll see this a lot with mobile homes,

Those usually default.
So I stay away from those.
- Unless you want them, right?
Unless you're like, yeah, I would love to own that.
- Exactly, that's what I'm saying.
Unless you really want to own it.
Like, okay, non-performing notes,

I'm probably going to end up owning this property very likely.
But ultimately the value of a real estate note
depends upon the economic conditions
that support the value of the property.
And say that again.
The value of the note,
there's a lot of factors, but the value of a note

that support the value of the property.
For example, an owner-occupied single family house
in a good neighborhood, in an area
with a diversified long-term stable economy
is about the best collateral you can get.
So that's what I look at.
Amortized note is more valuable than one with a balloon
'cause often the balloons aren't paid,
and they have to, you know-
- You're going to end with the product.
- Yeah, exactly.
