metadata.title: LAWYER: How to Protect Your "Subject-To" Deal From a Seller Bankruptcy!
metadata.author: Real Estate Law Guys I Asset Protection
metadata.shortDescription:
Subject-To Real Estate Deals: You closed the deal on your first “Subject To” Deal. The keys are in your hand. STR income is rolling in. And then you get a notice: The seller just filed for bankruptcy.

✅ Get YOUR Special Offer To Set Up Your LLC & Asset Protection NOW!
https://appointment.strlawguys.com/schedule-appointment/

PICK UP JEFF'S BEST-SELLING BOOK ON ASSET PROTECTION AT AMAZON:
https://a.co/d/3zC1Wx3

Suddenly, the deal you thought was done… might not be. In the eyes of the bankruptcy court? That house might not even be yours anymore.
You paid the seller.
You made the payments.
You furnished the Airbnb.

But the trustee wants it back. So—what the hell happens now? In this video, I’m walking you through the bankruptcy bomb that can explode in a Subject-To deal. You’ll learn what happens if the seller files, how long you’re exposed, and how to protect yourself using one specific document most investors don’t even know about.

SECTION 1 — The 90-Day Window That Can Kill Your Deal

Here’s the first thing to understand. If your seller files for bankruptcy within 90 days of your Subject-To closing, the court can try to reverse the entire deal. I’m not talking theory. This is federal law—Section 547 of the Bankruptcy Code. It’s called an avoidable preference. The trustee’s job is to unwind transactions that look suspicious—especially ones that benefit a single party right before a bankruptcy filing.

And guess what? Your Subject-To deal fits that profile. Even if everything was fair. Even if you paid arrears, paid cash, or cleaned up the property. If they file too soon after closing, the trustee can reclaim the house—and potentially erase everything you’ve done.

That means:
– You lose the title.
– You might not get reimbursed for improvements.
– And if you’ve got renters or STR bookings? Cancel ‘em. It’s not your property anymore.

This isn’t rare. It’s just rarely talked about. So how do you protect yourself?

SECTION 2 — Mitigation: Time + Structure = Survival

Your first defense is time. Make sure you’re not doing a Subject-To deal with someone who’s weeks away from bankruptcy.

Look for red flags.
– Multiple judgments?
– Tax liens?
– Collections or pending evictions?

If any of that shows up during due diligence… you’ve got a ticking clock.

Your second defense is how you structure the deal. And this is where most Subject-To investors screw up: They close informally. No note. No wraparound. No protections. But if you use a secured promissory note and a wraparound mortgage, everything changes.

SECTION 3 — Wraparound = Your Legal Safety Net

When you create a wraparound note, the seller becomes a secured creditor. If they file for bankruptcy later… That note becomes an asset in the estate.

That means:
✅ The trustee is more likely to honor the deal,
✅ You keep possession,
✅ And they may just collect payments or sell the note—not the house.

Compare that to a deal where the buyer’s just Venmoing mortgage payments each month. No contract? No protections. That’s not creative finance. That’s gambling.

SECTION 4 — Post-90-Day Bankruptcy: Still Dangerous

What if the seller files more than 90 days after you close? Usually, you’re in the clear.

But there are still traps:
– If you didn’t record the deed, the trustee can dispute ownership.
– If you’re related to the seller, it can be labeled insider dealing.
– If the trustee thinks it was a fraudulent conveyance, the deal could still be challenged.

So yes, post-90-day is safer. But only if you’ve got clean paperwork, clear value, and public record of the transfer.

SECTION 5 — The Bankruptcy Trigger You Didn’t Expect

Here’s one more risk most investors don’t see coming: When the seller files for bankruptcy, the lender gets notified. And that notification might reveal that the property was transferred. Which means… the bank can now enforce the due-on-sale clause.

Even if payments are current. Even if the deal was a year ago. Suddenly, they’ve got a reason—and the incentive—to accelerate the loan.

So if you’re sitting on a 3.2% fixed mortgage, and rates are at 7%. You’ve just become very interesting to that bank. This isn’t a certainty—but it’s always a risk.

That’s why experienced investors keep backup capital or financing available, just in case the bank calls the note.

SECTION 6 — Short-Term Rentals: Extra Risk, Extra Exposure

STRs are an amazing use for Subject-To deals. But they come with higher stakes.

Why?
– The value is often higher, which attracts trustee scrutiny.
– Improvements and furnishings may be lost if the deal is reversed.
– Local licensing or revenue may be frozen if ownership is contested.

And worst of all? You might not get a dime of that investment back.

So if you’re doing STRs Subject-To:
– Check for bankruptcy flags.
– Record the deed immediately.
– Wrap the deal with a note and mortgage.
– Keep 91+ days distance from any known distress.
– And always have a Plan B if the bank calls the loan.

metadata.title: The Note Investing Strategy for Busy W-2 Professionals with Sierra Davis
metadata.author: Agent2Investor Podcast
metadata.shortDescription:
This conversation delves into the intricacies of property financing, focusing on the roles of mortgage notes and seller financing. Sierra explains how financing works when purchasing property, the creation of promissory notes, and how these notes function as IOUs secured by the property. 
The discussion also highlights the benefits of receiving monthly payments through seller financing instead of direct property ownership.

metadata.title: Mortgage Note Investing Explained: The Non-Performing Loan Opportunity
metadata.author: PPR Capital Management
metadata.shortDescription:
What happens when a homeowner stops making mortgage payments? And why would an investment firm want to buy that loan?

In this masterclass, PPR Capital Management's Director of Non-Performing Loan Investments, Taylor Nelson, breaks down the world of non-performing loans (NPLs) and explains how mortgage debt can become an attractive investment opportunity.

You'll learn:

What non-performing loans are
Why banks sell distressed mortgage debt
How investors acquire and manage NPL portfolios
Real-world case studies from PPR's investment portfolio
How reperforming loans can create value
Common misconceptions about the NPL market
Why PPR continues to invest in this asset class today

Whether you're a real estate investor, accredited investor, or simply looking to better understand alternative investments, this masterclass provides an inside look at one of the largest segments of PPR Capital Management's investment platform.

About PPR Capital Management

PPR Capital Management is a private equity real estate investment firm with over $1.4 billion in assets under management and more than 2,000 investors nationwide. Since 2007, PPR has focused on identifying opportunities across residential mortgage debt, multifamily real estate, build-to-rent housing, and other alternative investment strategies.

Learn more at: https://pprcapitalmgmt.com/

metadata.title: PaperStac Marketplace & Mortgage Note Investing Guide

metadata.shortDescription:
Discover how PaperStac makes mortgage note investing easy and learn how to buy mortgage notes online with platform co-founders Brett Berkey and Rick Allen, alongside host Patrick Franz.

In this episode of the Real Men of Real Estate Radio Show, we explore how technology is revolutionizing alternative debt investing. Learn why savvy investors are stepping into the bank's shoes to collect monthly mortgage payments without the headaches of tenants, toilets, or maintenance. With billions in defaulted real estate debt hitting the secondary market, this episode reveals how individual investors can capitalize on the coming wave.

Brett and Rick walk through the PaperStac marketplace, demonstrating how their automated closing engine streamlines due diligence, collateral files, assignments, and secure transactions. By combining expert training like Note Investor University with intuitive software, buying and selling paper real estate has never been more accessible.

Key Takeaways:
The Landlord Alternative: Why collecting mortgage payments as a lender beats physical property management and maintenance.

The Coming Debt Wave: Identifying upcoming opportunities as billions in defaulted real estate debt hit the secondary market.

Automated Trading: How the PaperStac platform guides buyers and sellers through due diligence, collateral files, and secure closings.

Software Meets Education: Combining strategic training with digital tools to safely execute paper real estate deals online.

Connect with Patrick Franz (The Note Mentor): https://linktr.ee/pfranz79

If you found value in this deep dive into automated note trading, make sure to Like this video, drop a comment below with your biggest takeaway, and Subscribe to the channel! Hit the notification bell so you never miss an episode on mastering alternative real estate investing.

metadata.title: Should You Invest in a Mortgage Note Fund or Buy Notes Yourself?
metadata.author: Paperstac
metadata.shortDescription:
Should you invest in a mortgage note fund or build your own portfolio of mortgage notes?

In this episode of the Paperstac Podcast, Brett Burky and Rick Allen break down one of the most common questions in the note investing industry: Is it better to invest passively through a mortgage note fund or actively purchase mortgage notes yourself?

Both strategies can generate attractive returns, passive income, and portfolio diversification, but they come with very different levels of risk, control, liquidity, and time commitment.

In this episode, you'll learn:

✅ What a mortgage note fund is

✅ How mortgage note funds generate returns

✅ The benefits of passive investing

✅ The advantages of owning mortgage notes directly

✅ Risk factors investors should consider

✅ How much control you have in each strategy

✅ Expected returns and investment structures

✅ Which strategy may be best for beginners

✅ How experienced investors use both approaches

Whether you're looking for passive income, alternative investments, retirement portfolio diversification, or ways to build long-term wealth, understanding the differences between mortgage note funds and direct note investing is critical before deploying capital.

Topics Covered:

* Mortgage Note Funds
* Note Investing
* Mortgage Notes
* Passive Income
* Alternative Investments
* Real Estate Investing
* Seller Financing
* Distressed Debt
* Private Lending
* Investment Funds
* Cash Flow Investing
* Retirement Investing
* Self-Directed IRAs
* Wealth Building Strategies
* Real Estate Notes

By the end of this episode, you'll have a clear understanding of the pros and cons of each approach and be better equipped to decide whether passive investing through a fund or actively buying mortgage notes aligns with your investment goals.

metadata.shortDescription:
Get ready for another captivating episode of the "My First Note" series, where we take a deep dive into the exciting world of mortgage note investing alongside the incredible Tracy Rewey. Tracy, a renowned expert in the note investing space, brings a wealth of experience and success to the table as both an experienced note investor and educator in the note investing industry.

In this episode, Tracy shares her experience and insights on her very first mortgage note purchase. Sharing invaluable insights and personal stories that will keep you hooked from start to finish. 

With a background in title and real estate closing, Tracy's journey into note investing began when she joined a company that bought seller-financed real estate notes. After years of working in the industry, she and her husband decided to start their own note investing company in 1997.

In this episode, Tracy discusses her initial exposure to the financial calculator and her transition from the document realm to the investment realm. She shares how she used notes differently at first, focusing on buying and selling real estate with seller financing. 

Tracy explains her first note deal, which involved purchasing an REO property in Spokane, Washington. She also reveals how she creatively utilized seller financing for a fourplex property, implementing a house hacking strategy before it had a name.

Throughout the conversation, Tracy emphasizes the opportunities present in the current market for buying and selling seller-financed properties. With rising interest rates, she believes there is significant potential to purchase properties at a lower price and sell them at a higher price with seller financing. Tracy encourages viewers to think beyond buying existing notes and consider the possibilities of creating their own notes as either a buyer or seller.

Join us as we uncover Tracy's valuable insights, personal anecdotes, and expert advice that will inspire and educate both new and seasoned investors in the captivating realm of note investing. Don't miss out on this exciting opportunity to learn from one of the industry's finest!

If you're interested in mortgage notes, and gaining valuable tips from a seasoned investor, don't miss this episode with Tracy Rewey. Discover how she embarked on her note investing journey, learn about her first note purchases, and gain insights into the current market conditions that favor seller financing strategies.

metadata.title: Buying Houses Subject To The Existing Mortgage | Sub To Real Estate Investing
metadata.author: Lex Levinrad Real Estate Training and Coaching
metadata.shortDescription:
BUYING HOUSES SUBJECT TO THE EXISTING MORTGAGE "SUBJECT TO"

In the previous video I spoke about seller financing and how to use this strategy when a seller owns a property free and clear. 

In this video I explain how buying houses subject to the existing mortgage works. Many people abbreviate this to "subject to" or "sub to". All it means is that you are taking over the payments of the seller and buying the house subject to the existing mortgage that is in place. You are essentially assuming their mortgage. 

Whenever you encounter a seller that has a mortgage, is current on their payments and has a low interest rate, you should be trying to negotiate a subject to offer where you can buy the house subject to the existing mortgage and take over their mortgage payments.

Many people think that buying houses subject to is illegal. It is not. However there is something called a "due on sale" clause that you should be aware of. This clause means that the lender can call the loan due in 30 days if the property is sold or conveyed. There are ways of getting around this restriction. Buying houses subject to is perfectly legal and is also a great way to buy real estate because you can buy unlimited amounts of real estate. Traditional lenders will only let you have 10 houses in your own name. However, when you are buying houses subject to you can buy as many houses as you want. 

When you are talking to motivated sellers, you always want to know if they are current on their mortgage, how much they owe on the mortgage, how long is left on the mortgage (years) and what the interest rate is. You also want to know what the monthly mortgage payment is (including taxes and insurance). The ideal scenario is a property that needs no work, has a low payment (like $1,000) and could be rented for a much higher amount (like $2,000). 

You may think that this is difficult to find but there are many sellers that purchased a home in 2021 or 2022 that have very low interest rates on their mortgages (some are less than 3%). Let's say you meet a motivated seller who has a mortgage and is current on their mortgage. You should immediately be thinking about creating a subject to offer. The best way to do this is by price anchoring low with your cash offer and then making the subject to offer sound more appealing. If this is absolutely rejected you can go back to the cash offer and increase the offer amount. 

Here is an example of buying a house subject to:

A seller wants to sell their house for 200k. They call you from a postcard that you mailed to a list of owner occupied homes. Your cash offer as an investor is 120k cash. They immediately reject your offer. 

You ask more questions and find out that they have a mortgage and they owe $150k to the bank. 

You offer to buy their house and give them $10,000 as a down payment and take over the existing mortgage that they have ($150,000). Your offer is now 160k.

Initially they don't like the idea, because they have a realtor that can bring them a buyer at 170k. But you point out to them that even if they sold for $170,000 after commissions and closing costs they would be walking away with 153k and since they owe $150 they would essentially be getting $3,000 (versus your offer of $10,000 cash up front). 

They agree and you buy the house with just $10,000 down. 

With subject to, in some cases, you can persuade someone to sell their house without putting any money down at all. A true no money down. 

For example what if their mortgage balance was $170,000?

And they had an offer they were considering through a realtor for $170,000. If they sell at $170,000 with an agent and pay 6% commission and 4% in closing costs they would only net 153k.  but they owe the bank $170,000 which means they would need to come out of pocket and write a check to the title company for $17,000 at closing!

But you are offering to buy their house and take over the mortgage and they get to just "walk away". Do you see how that could be appealing to some sellers? And if the interest rate on their mortgage is low then that could be a win win and be really good for you as an investor too!

In today's market, learning how to buy houses subject to the existing mortgage is very important since prices have pulled back around 15% and the typical buyer that put 5% or 10% down is not able to sell and pay off their mortgage. But if they have good credit they may have a sub 3% mortgage which could be taken over! It's just waiting to be assumed!

I teach creative financing methods like buying houses subject to the existing mortgage, subject to real estate investing strategies and creative financing methods like seller financing at the Foreclosures, Short Sales and Bank Owned Properties Boot Camp. 

You can learn more about that boot camp at this link: 

https://www.lexlevinrad.com/foreclosures-bank-owned-properties-boot-camp/

metadata.shortDescription:
Pace Morby goes on a seller call at a potential investment property to explain subject to and build rapport with the seller. The value of the home is less than what the seller owes, meaning if they sold the house they’d have to cut a check in order to walk away. As an investor the most important part of the deal is securing the mortgage rate already in place, which is Pace’s aim in taking on a property like this.

metadata.title: How To Buy Houses Subject To The Existing Mortgage Explained in Detail
metadata.author: Lex Levinrad Real Estate Training and Coaching
metadata.shortDescription:
In this video, I explain how buying houses subject to the existing mortgage works. Buying houses "Subject To" which is often abbreviated to "Sub To" is a very powerful strategy especially in today's market where rates have moved from 3% to 8%. 

Buying a house subject to the existing mortgage essentially means that you are agreeing to buy the house and assume the sellers mortgage. As an example, if you agreed to buy a house for $350,000 and the seller owed the bank $350,000 you could agree to buy the house subject to that existing $350,000 mortgage. 

If you purchased the house in the above example, as an investor your cash out of pocket would be zero. Why would a seller agree to this? Most sellers wouldn't, but if your seller is motivated to sell, or they have been trying to sell and have not been able to sell, then they may consider agreeing to this strategy. 

In Today's market, many sellers are unrealistic about what their property is worth. They still think it's worth what Zillow said it was worth 12 months ago (or what they heard a neighbor down the street sold their house for). But when they decide to list their property for sale, they are surprised to see that they are not getting any offers. And the reason they are not getting any offers is because the market has changed. 

Prices have come down from what Zillow said their house was worth 12 months ago. And since interest rates have increased from 3% to 8%, many buyers that would have qualified for a mortgage to buy their house can no longer qualify for a mortgage because the payment is too high and it exceeds their debt to income ratio. 

Some sellers have a buyer sign a purchase contract and are waiting to close when they find out 3 weeks before closing that their buyer didn't qualify for a mortgage. 

At this point, the seller begins to get worried. The typical seller has already started packing up the contents of their house in boxes. It did not occur to them that the buyer may not qualify for a mortgage. When they find out that the buyer is not buying their house, the seller may begin to worry about selling their house. If the realtor has reduced the listing price before they got an offer they become even more concerned, especially if they see listings in their neighborhood being reduced (or more houses being listed for sale).

This worry is exacerbated by the fact that they have already packed up most of their house and already have somewhere that they are moving to (like a new house that they are buying). They are essentially committed to leaving the house and now need it sold. What are they going to tell their kids? So they tell the realtor to lower the price again.  

And their property sits on the MLS for 30, 60, or even 90 days with no offers. Their agent tells them to reduce the price again and they agree. Meantime, prices are coming down and the seller begins to realize that they would be lucky to sell the house and pay off the mortgage after factoring in commissions, closing costs etc. 

As an example, assume that the seller had a house that they wanted to sell for $400,000. And let's say they had a mortgage balance of $350,000. The commission of 6% on a $400,000 sale is $24,000. Closing costs of around 2.5% would be an additional fee of $10,000. 

Buyers are required to complete an "Inspection" on a property prior to agreeing to buy it to make sure that there is nothing wrong with the roof, plumbing, electrical, AC, etc. Typically there will be some items that are required to be repaired which the seller may either repair themselves or agree to give a credit to the buyer for the amount of repairs. A credit of $5,000 would be typical on a $400,000 house. 

So if the seller listed their house for $400,000 and had a mortgage of $350,000, they would only walk away with $11,000 if they got a full price offer!

See the breakdown below:

Sales Price                 $400,000
Payoff Mortgage       $350,000
Less commission      $24,000
Less closing costs    $10,000
Less Credit to buyer  $5,000

Net Cash To Seller    $11,000

So what would happen if the buyer fell through because they could not qualify for a mortgage and they reduced the price to say $390,000 and found a buyer? The seller would net zero! They would essentially be walking away with nothing. What if their best offer was $375,000. 

They would have to PAY $15,000 to sell their house!
      
And at this point, that is where a seller will be motivated enough to consider this strategy since they are motivated to sell and there is no other way that they can sell and walk away. 

If you are going to buy houses subject to their existing mortgage you need to do it correctly. 

You need to hire an attorney to handle all of the paperwork and the closing. 

And you need to be able to explain to the seller how this strategy works. 

*This is not to be construed as legal advice. Please consult with your attorney*

Watch the video to learn how to buy houses subject to the existing mortgage

It also may prevent you from getting another mortgage and can damage your credit badly. Stay away from creative financing!

metadata.title: How to explain a subject to real estate deal to a seller
metadata.author: kris haskins
metadata.shortDescription:
Today we're talking to a motivated seller to explain how to buy their house using the creative real estate strategy called "Subject To".  This is where we buy the house, but we leave the mortgage in the seller's name.  But there's a specific way we must explain this strategy to sellers because we can't use industry jargon when we're negotiating.  All we want to do is transfer our beliefs of buying real estate over to our seller.  Watch and listen to the questions we ask and how we set up the deal w/out overcomplicating the phone call conversation.  You’ll hear exactly how I talk to homeowners and how I explain creative financing in a way that makes sense to them. No banks. No loan applications. No credit checks.

That's why we'll need our seller to sign specific documents allowing us to speak about their home loan.  Today I'm calling to find out WHY I haven't received any paper statements in the mail and also find out WHY my monthly payment went DOWN. metadata.shortDescription:
Pace Morby joins Kevin Choe in front of a duplex Kevin bought part subject to at 4.25% and 0% seller financing. They break down the deal, where it came from, who’s making money on it, and HOW it will cash flow every month. Kevin talks about the benefits of buying duplexes over single-family homes. They dive into the specific numbers on this real estate investment and where each figure came from.

Yes, it is possible to buy real estate without using your own money, credit, tax returns, or having a W-2. Stay tuned for the second part of this video where Kevin and Eric will be walking the property, discussing renovation plans, and how much everything will cost Kevin in the end.

metadata.title: Using an Installment Sale to Reduce Taxes - When Selling Your Business
metadata.author: Ironclad Wealth Management
metadata.shortDescription:
Time is your greatest ally when it comes to saving taxes. By spreading payments over time, you can potentially lower your immediate tax burden and have more control over when you are taxed. 

This video explains how installment sales work and why they can be a powerful tax strategy for business owners. 

What you'll learn:
 • What an installment sale is and how it works
 • The tax advantages of spreading income over multiple years
 • Key rules and considerations before setting up an installment sale
 • How this strategy fits into long-term wealth and exit planning

Whether you’re preparing to sell your business, real estate, or other major assets, understanding installment sales can help you keep more of what you’ve earned. 

Want to learn more? Schedule a call! https://www.ironcladwm.com/talk-with-an-advisor

metadata.title: Structured Installment Sales - Eliminate Buyer Risk While Deferring Taxes
metadata.author: Ironclad Wealth Management
metadata.shortDescription:
Selling your business or a highly appreciated asset can create a massive tax bill, but with the right planning, you don’t have to pay it all at once. A Structured Installment Sale allows you to defer taxes, spread income over time, and reduce risk compared to a traditional installment sale.

This video explains how Structured Installment Sales work and why they can be a powerful strategy for business owners looking to exit with confidence.

What you'll learn:
• What a Structured Installment Sale is and how it differs from a standard installment sale
• How this strategy helps defer capital gains taxes and improve cash flow 
• Ways to eliminate payment risk by using a structured approach
• How Structured Installment Sales fit into a long-term wealth and retirement plan 

If you’re a business owner preparing to sell, this strategy may help you protect your wealth, reduce uncertainty, and create more financial freedom after your exit.

Want to learn more? Schedule a call! https://www.ironcladwm.com/talk-with-an-advisor

metadata.title: Title Company vs Law Firm: Best Way to Close Subject‑To & Wraps
metadata.author: Scott Horne's Owner Finance Network
metadata.shortDescription:
Confused about whether to close your subject‑to or wraparound deal at a title company or a law firm? Scott breaks down the real differences—who drafts what, what escrow officers can/can’t do, when title insurance is available, and how compliance (SAFE Act, Dodd‑Frank, state disclosures) actually fits into your closing.

You’ll learn
When a “title company closing” is really a law‑firm closing (no title policy)
Who can legally prepare notes/deeds and explain provisions
How to get title insurance on creative deals (and when you can’t)
Why compliance & disclosures matter (and who helps you stay clean)
How to pick the right closing partner and avoid dead‑deal surprises

If this helped, please like, comment, and subscribe—it tells the algorithm other investors need this too.

00:00 Intro: Title Co vs Law Firm (Creative Finance)

For more info on underwriting seller finance loans or get started on a deal go to www.calltheunderwriter.com.

metadata.title: 12 Questions to Ask a Title Company Before You Send a Subject-To or Creative Finance Deal
metadata.author: Music City TC
metadata.shortDescription:
Before you send your next creative deal to a title company, ask these 12 questions. The answers tell you whether the file will close smoothly or fall apart in week three.

In this episode of Contract to Close, Stephanie, Lead Transaction Coordinator at Music City TC, walks through the questions in four groups:
- Experience: how many subject-to, seller finance and wrap closings they've done, who handles them, and what their underwriter requires
- Documents: what they need to open the file, who drafts the deed, note and deed of trust, and how they handle a seller power of attorney
- The closing: how the existing loan shows on the settlement statement, how reinstatement works, and how liens and judgments get cleared
- Logistics: signing options, fees, wire fraud protection, and communication
Plus the red flags that mean you should keep looking.

Got a deal under contract? Two ways to reach us:
Book a 20-minute deal call: https://calendly.com/stephanie-musiccitytc/deal-call
Or email the crew: hello@musiccitytc.com

More from Contract to Close:
Ep 1, What Happens After Your Subject-To Contract Is Signed: https://youtu.be/7bRWKlhJ1Gs
Ep 2, Subject-To Insurance: https://youtu.be/APP2agDO8mY

Free Creative Close Checklist: https://musiccitytc.com/resources
Website: https://musiccitytc.com

This video is general education, not legal advice. Every state and title company is different. Work through the specifics of every deal with your title company and attorney.

Music City TC: we run the show behind your closing.

metadata.title: How Owner Financing Works in Texas: Step-by-Step (Buyer & Seller Guide)
metadata.author: Greg Schwartz | Investing in Bryan-College Station
metadata.shortDescription:
Seller financing offers a strategic way to bridge the gap between buyers and sellers, creating win-win outcomes.

This breakdown covers how this creative finance strategy works for real estate investors. You will learn the mechanics behind these agreements, why they are often misunderstood, and how to navigate the complexities safely. We discuss the essential process of buyer vetting to ensure your interests remain protected throughout the transaction.

Whether you are concerned about pre-payment penalties or simply want to understand the flexibility owner financing provides, this overview clarifies the steps involved. Proper documentation is key to maintaining security, and I explain how to structure these deals effectively to benefit both parties.

Subscribe for weekly real estate strategy breakdowns, and comment below if you have specific questions about structuring your next deal.

00:00 - Introduction to Seller Financing
00:37 - The 5 Steps of Seller Financing
00:50 - Step 1: Negotiations & Loan Terms
02:24 - Balloon Payments vs. Prepayment Penalties
04:10 - Step 2: Crafting the Contract & Addendum
05:16 - Step 3: Vetting & Underwriting the Buyer
06:16 - Step 4: Title, Promissory Notes & Closing
07:26 - Step 5: Loan Servicing & How Deals Conclude
08:48 - Additional Seller Financing Resources

Reach out!
Call / Text 443-812-0357
Email info@schwartzrealtygroup.com

I'm Greg Schwartz, a real estate investor and agent in Bryan/College Station, TX. Helping Bryan, Texas and College Station Texas, landlords buy, sell, and self-manage for maximum rental profit.
📩 Deal of the Week Newsletter: http://subscribepage.io/36Ch3a 
🌐 Website: www. schwartzrealtygroup.com

Keller Williams Brazos Valley

Are you wondering what the key differences are between Subject-To and Wraparound Mortgages? In this video, I break down the two biggest differences between these creative real estate financing strategies, so you can use them to grow your real estate portfolio without relying on banks!

✅ What You’ll Learn in This Video:

What Subject-To investing is and how it works
How Wraparound Mortgages function in real estate deals
The #1 mistake new investors make with these strategies
Which method is better for cash flow and risk management
Both of these strategies allow you to buy houses with little to no money down, but choosing the right one can mean the difference between profit and loss. Whether you’re a beginner or an experienced investor, understanding these differences will give you an edge in closing more deals and building long-term wealth.

If you’re serious about real estate investing and want to master creative financing, watch this video until the end!

Is it possible to overcome the due on sale clause in a subject to deal? In this video, I'll discuss overcoming the due on sale clause on a subject to deal. In addition, I’ll show you how to get paid four times from the same deal. 

A subject to deal in real estate refers to a property that is not yet fully owned by the buyer. In other words, the seller retains some ownership of the property until a certain date or condition has been met. This can be done in many ways, but it usually involves selling the house to someone else and then having them sell it again to you at some point in time. 

Learn more about how to become anonymous AND appear as if you own nothing at our next Free Tax & Asset Protection Workshop. Save Your Seat: https://aba.link/2d9

To those buying a subject to deal, be sure to watch this video! I'll teach you how to get around the due on sale clause and make the most of your purchase. From negotiation tactics to using strategies, I'll show you everything you need to know to get the best deal on a subject to deal!

When buying subject to deals, the seller will often include a due on sale clause. Meaning that if you don't take the subject within a certain number of days of the sale, the seller can resell the subject to someone else.

Although this might seem like a difficult clause to overcome, you can do a few things to make it easier. First, make sure you understand the clause and what it means. Next, is to gather the best information possible to help you navigate through the process. Finally, watch this video to learn more about what powers you have in this scenario.

metadata.author: William Tingle
metadata.shortDescription:
Everyone talks about the due-on-sale clause when it comes to Subject-To deals, but that’s not the biggest risk you should be worried about. 

In this video, we dive deep into the hidden risks of Sub2 investing that rarely get mentioned. If you’re doing or planning to do creative real estate deals, you need to hear this.

Key Takeaways:

✨The overlooked Sub2 risk that could impact your deal long-term.
✨Why a common mistake investors make can cost them thousands.
✨What smart investors do to protect themselves beyond the paperwork.

Do you want to learn about the one strategic shift that completely simplified my investing business and made me more money? Check out my new book The 12 House Blueprint.

This book demystifies real estate investing, breaking down strategies that don’t require traditional financing, hefty savings, or perfect credit. Whether you’re completely new to real estate or looking for a smarter approach, this book gives you a clear, achievable plan to build wealth and control your time.

Learn more here: http://www.12houseblueprintbook.com

⚠️⚠️ DISCLAIMER ⚠️⚠️
William is not a CPA, attorney, insurance expert, contractor, lender, or financial advisor. Tell the truth...he only completed the 9th grade in high school. For the above reasons...the information shared in these videos should not be considered tax, legal, insurance, construction, engineering, health & safety, electrical, financial advice, or anything else of that nature. It may be outdated or inaccurate, and it is your responsibility to verify all details on your own. This video is intended for educational purposes ONLY.

metadata.title: I Had The Due-On-Sale Clause Called on My Subject-To Deal (Real Story)
metadata.author: Evan Ragsdale
metadata.shortDescription:
We actually had a due-on-sale clause called on a subject-to deal.

Not something I heard about.
Not a theory.
A real situation we had to navigate.

In this video, I walk through exactly what happened, why we believe it was triggered, and how we handled it in a way that protected the homeowner, kept the deal intact, and avoided panic or bad decisions. This deal involved a large mortgage servicer, payments were current, and the issue didn’t come from what most people expect — which is why understanding exposure, insurance, and structure matters more than pretending risk doesn’t exist.

I also explain why subject-to deals can still be powerful when done correctly, how a contract for deed allowed us to restructure the deal without changing title on public record, and the biggest lesson most investors miss when they hear “due-on-sale.”

This video isn’t meant to scare you — it’s meant to give clarity, especially if you’re doing or considering creative finance deals in the real world.

👇 If you want deeper conversations like this
I run a community where we break down subject-to deals, wraps, contracts for deed, and real scenarios that don’t always go perfectly — honestly and without hype.

👉 Join here:
https://www.skool.com/creativefinancemastery/about?ref=9c70e45ac96b4177a5ab2b0d68e551f9

If this video helped, hit like, subscribe, and drop a comment — I read every one.

Episode #206

For the past few years, “subject to” real estate has been all the rage. Everyone is talking about how they scored a great real estate deal by taking over a seller’s rock-bottom interest rate mortgage payment. You see it all over social media, “I got this house for zero dollars down with a three percent mortgage rate!” And while this may seem too good to be true, the practice of subject to real estate isn’t illegal, but some of its huge risks could ruin an inexperienced real estate investor. 

So, who do we have on to talk about subject to? Eddie Speed! Eddie is a creative financing master who’s been in the real estate note investing business for over forty years. Eddie has been around the block more than most and has seen the good and bad sides of subject to real estate. It’s become alarming to Eddie how many inexperienced investors are using this strategy without knowing the risks, putting their wealth and, more importantly, sellers in danger by being far too cavalier about the massive downsides of getting this real estate strategy wrong.

Eddie walks through exactly how subject to works, the one clause that could blow up your entire deal, what will trigger it, the difference between subject to and assumable loans, who should be using subject to, and who DEFINITELY shouldn’t. Even if you’ve done a subject to deal before, you’d better stick around for this one, because you may have gotten it wrong.

metadata.title: Transferring Property to an LLC: Don't Fear the Due On Sale Clause
metadata.author: Ken McElroy
metadata.shortDescription:
Join Ken's Inner Circle and join other like-minded real estate entrepreneurs in the Inner Circle Forum. Follow this link: https://kenmcelroy.com/join

Mauricio Rauld, Ken McElroy's Legal Advisor, breaks down the concept of the "due on sale" clause in loan agreements. Mauricio addresses common fears surrounding the clause and sheds light on its history, impact, and why most borrowers shouldn't worry about its impact. Check out Mauricio’s channel: https://YouTube.com/@mauriciorauldesq

Ken has a real estate strategies podcast! Subscribe on your favorite platform to get each week's episode.
Apple Podcasts: https://apple.co/3jDqftx
Spotify: https://spoti.fi/31GUDwW

Follow Ken on the X social media platform at: https://x.com/kenmcelroy

• • •

Be sure to click the bell to be notified as soon as the next informational video is posted!

Visit Ken's Bookstore: https://kenmcelroy.com/books/

•
ABOUT KEN:
Ken is the author of the bestselling books The ABC’s of Real Estate Investing, The Advanced Guide to Real Estate Investing, The ABC’s of Property Management, and has an upcoming book: "ABCs of Buying Rental Property: How You Can Achieve Financial Freedom in Five Years." Ken is a Rich Dad Advisor. 
   

Ken offers a wealth of personal experiences, practical advice, success stories, and even some informative setbacks, all presented here to educate and inspire. Whether you’re a new or seasoned investor, the information and resources on this channel will set you on a path where you and your investments can thrive.

Ken's company: https://mccompanies.com/

which in my opinion, as a former asset protection attorney, is not something
you should be afraid of or be as fearful as most of you are.
Quite simply, a do on sale clause is a provision in the loan agreement
that gives the lender the right but not the obligation to call your loan.
If you transfer the property from your name into somebody else's.
While many real estate
investors transfer their properties from their personal name over to LLC.
A lot of them still remain fearful that the do on sale clause
will be calling them.
And a lot of you guys are actually so fearful
that you actually don't transfer the property from your personal name
into the LLC for fear of the lender calling your loan.
So what do we have do on sale clauses to begin with?
This all started really from the lenders back in the 1980s when mortgage rates
skyrocketed to about 18% and people were starting to transfer
their properties to other people.
Keeping the current loan in place.
So, for example, you would have somebody who owned
a piece of property and let's say their loan was 4% at the time
and they wanted to transfer or sell that property to somebody.
Well, if the interest rate was 18%, what people started to do
was to transfer title to the property from.
From you to the new buyer.
But they would keep this loan in place so that the new buyer
only was paying the 4% as opposed to the new 8%.
Sometimes you call this a wrap,
but essentially the loan stayed in place even though the title transfer.
So lenders got wind of this and started putting language in the loan agreements
that actually prohibited them from doing that
and triggered this ability of the lenders to call the loan
if there was a transfer from one party to another.
So one of the things you want to understand is actually two
scenarios were the do on sale clause apply.
So in scenario number one is the scenario that really the lenders
are really concerned about, which is when you own a piece of property
and you're trying to sell your property to a third party.
Now, remember, the lender in this case has done its due diligence on
you, has underwritten you has checked your credit score, is comfortable
with your ability to pay the mortgage and therefore extended you the loan.
However, when you transfer that to a third party,
if you tried to keep that loan in place, will the lender now has a new credit risk?
They don't know anything about this party.
They don't know if they're credit worthy.
And so they have a concern, a legitimate concern, in my opinion,
about the ability of the new buyer to pay the loan.
So it makes sense that the lenders would be concerned about this
and have a provision in their agreements for this.
So even in this scenario, lenders aren't inclined to call the loan,
even when they know a third party has come into play.
For example, one of my good friends, Paice Moorby,
who is probably one of the more foremost
experts in the subject to industry, does these kinds of deals all the time.
And he talks openly about how he's done over a thousand of these.
And even in these scenarios, he's only had the due on sale clause issue
around five times, which I do the math is about half a percent of the time.
That's even becomes an issue.
And in every time he's actually been able to work something out with the bank.
So it's not something that happens all the time and the risk is probably
very small that the bank would even call the loan even in this scenario.
So that scenario one, but the scenario
that we are most concerned about, which is transferring our properties
from our personal names into our own LLC, is actually a separate issue.
It's not transferring property from my personal name into a third party,
sort of an arm's length transaction.
I'm actually transferring it into an LLC that is owned by me.
I'm just transferring it for asset protection purposes.
And this is something that's quite different
because unlike the first scenario in this scenario,
I still am the main owner of the LLC and I'm still responsible for the loan
and the lender's already underwritten.
Me is comfortable with my ability to repay.
So simply transferring it into an LLC that I own that has the same ownership
as this property is less of a concern to the lender.
So much so that both Fannie Mae and Freddie Mac actually have guidelines
in scenarios like this.
When you're transferring properties from your personal name
into the names of the LLC and both Freddie Mac and Fannie Mae's guidelines
instruct the lenders not to call the loan when it's a scenario
like this where you're simply transferring it into the LLC.
Fannie Mae.
These regulations reads The lender must process the following exempt transaction.
A transfer of the property to an LLC provided that a
the mortgage loan was purchased or securitized by Fannie Mae on
or after June 1st, 2016, and the LLC is controlled by the original borrower,
or the original borrower owns a majority interest in that LLC.
And furthermore, in situations where all of the following conditions are
met, Freddie Mac will permit a transfer of ownership of the mortgage premises.
The transfer is to an LLC, provided that the managing member
is the original borrower, and if there are multiple borrowers,
all of them must be members or partners of the LLC
and at least one of them must be a managing member.
As you can see, even Fannie Mae and Freddie Mac agree that
when you transfer the property into an LLC that is the same
original borrower of the same owner, the property is the same owner of the LLC,
then the bank is not supposed to execute on their due on sale clause.
So to be safe, make sure that the ownership
of the property matches the ownership to the LLC.
So if it's just you on the original deed, make sure you're the only one in the LLC.
If it's you and your spouse or you and your business partners,
make sure you guys are the same owners of the LLC and the same percentages.
And I think if you do that, you shouldn't have to fear about the due on sale clause
and think about it.

metadata.title: Non QM Mortgage Loan Explained | 3 Ways Self Employed Borrowers Can Qualify
metadata.author: Dani Rudd
metadata.shortDescription:
Self-employed and having trouble qualifying for a mortgage? Non-QM mortgage loans may offer financing solutions when traditional lending guidelines don't reflect your full financial picture.

In this video, I explain three alternative mortgage options that may help self-employed borrowers, business owners, and independent contractors qualify for home financing.

We cover:

Bank Statement Loans: Using eligible business or personal deposits to calculate qualifying income.

1099 Mortgage Programs: Alternative income documentation for independent contractors and self-employed professionals.

Asset-Based Qualification and Income Stacking: Using eligible assets and multiple income sources to strengthen mortgage qualification.

Non-QM loans can provide additional flexibility for borrowers who don't fit traditional Conventional, FHA, or VA lending guidelines. Loan requirements, down payments, interest rates, and documentation vary by program.

I'm Dani Rudd, Senior Loan Officer with Legacy Mutual Mortgage. With over 11 years of residential mortgage experience, I help homebuyers, homeowners, and real estate investors explore financing solutions tailored to their goals.

My experience includes VA, FHA, Conventional, USDA, Non-QM, DSCR investment property loans, and down payment assistance programs.

Have questions about your specific financing scenario? Contact my team or explore your options here:

https://legacymutual.com/officers/dani-rudd/

Dani Rudd | Senior Loan Officer
Legacy Mutual Mortgage
NMLS #1429254

#NonQM #SelfEmployedMortgage #BankStatementLoans #MortgageTips

metadata.title: THE 3% INTEREST HACK: Subject-To vs. Wrap Mortgages Explained
metadata.author: Ashland Mortgage
metadata.shortDescription:
we’re breaking down the two most powerful ways to "steal" a low interest rate in 2026. If you want to buy a house today but can't stand the 7% or 8% market rates, you need to understand the difference between a "Subject-To" deal and a "Wraparound Mortgage."

One lets you take over payments exactly as they are, while the other allows the seller to act as the bank and make a profit on the interest spread. We show you the legal structures, the risks of the "Due on Sale" clause, and which strategy gives you the most leverage as a savvy homebuyer.

In this video:

Subject-To: Taking over the existing loan "as is."

The Wrap: Creating a new, larger loan that "wraps around" the old one.

The Interest Spread: How sellers make money without even owning the house anymore.

Risk Management: Why you need a land trust or an LLC to stay under the radar.

#SubjectTo #WrapMortgage #CreativeFinancing #TheSavvyHomebuyer #RealEstate2026 #InterestRateHack #MortgageStrategy #DuaneBuziak

buying houses with low interest rates

do if they catch wind of the title
transfer, though this is rarely enforced
if the payments stay on time.

the bank from triggering a red flag in
their automated systems. Mastering these
two creative financing pillars allows
you to buy real estate in any
market condition because you aren't

are simply choosing the rates you want
to pay.

metadata.author: Dom Inglese
metadata.shortDescription:
Banks are saying “no” to more good families than ever… but those same families can still afford a house payment.

In this whiteboard session, I break down my #1 creative finance play – the wrap strategy – where I buy a house with a low-interest mortgage in place and then “wrap” that loan with a new, higher-interest loan to a non-bank-qualified buyer.

The result?

The buyer becomes a homeowner instead of a lifelong renter
I get paid upfront and every month from the interest rate spread
And we move one more family closer to the American dream of ownership instead of just survival.
If you want to help families banks reject and build real cash flow, you need to understand wraps.

In this Wrap Strategy Real Estate Explained video, I walk you through the full story with Johnny (the seller) and a non-bank-qualified buyer, so you can see the entire flow:

Step 1 – Buying with subject-to / seller finance
We start with Johnny, who has a low fixed-rate mortgage on his house. Using the subject-to strategy, I buy his property and take title while leaving his low-interest loan in place. Now Johnny’s house is my house – I own it, and I’ve stepped into his great financing.

Step 2 – Who the wrap buyer is (non-bank-qualified buyer)
Next, I look for a buyer who:

Can comfortably afford the monthly payment,

But can’t qualify for traditional financing because of things like cash-heavy income, a missed payment, credit dings, or not having the full down payment the bank wants.
These are the middle-class families stuck in the gap – great income, blocked by bank guidelines.

Step 3 – The numbers on a real wrap deal
I use simple numbers on the whiteboard:

I sell it to my buyer for more than I paid (typically 10–20% higher) with a higher interest rate and a solid down payment
This gives me profit on day one from the down payment difference and sets up my ongoing cash flow.

Step 4 – How the wrap actually works
I create a new note and mortgage to my buyer at, say, 7–8% interest, and that new loan “wraps” the original low-rate loan that’s still in place.

My buyer pays me each month at the higher rate
I keep making the lower-rate payment on the original loan
My cash flow is the spread between the two interest rates and payment amounts.

Step 5 – Why the buyer is happy (and wins big long-term)
The buyer:

Becomes a homeowner now instead of renting for another decade

Has a 30-year fixed, amortizing mortgage, so every payment builds equity

Potentially ends up with a paid-off house in 30 years that could be worth hundreds of thousands of dollars more than what they paid.
That equity becomes their nest egg, versus having nothing to show for a lifetime of rent.

Step 6 – Why this is my main strategy & mission
I explain why wraps are my quintessential strategy to “bring back the American dream for the middle class” – by helping families own earlier in life, so they’re not waiting until they’re nearly retirement age to finally have a home paid off. This is how we make homeownership possible again when the system says no.

If you’re an investor, wholesaler, or agent who wants to:

Turn dead leads into deals by helping buyers banks reject
Get paid upfront, every month, and on the back end
Use wraps, subject-to, and seller finance to create win–win homeownership…

👉 Comment “WRAP” if you want more breakdowns like this.

👉 Submit a deal or apply to work with us if you want help structuring wraps and creative finance offers on real properties

Stay tuned!

We'll guide you through the ups and downs of note investing and teach you all about the nitty-gritty details of the business that other people won't talk about. Your host, Dan Deppen, is a former aerospace engineer and product manager who transitioned away from cubicle life to full-time note investing in 2018. Our website is www.fusionnotes.com, where you can subscribe to this podcast, comment, and find links to other information on note investing. Hey everyone, welcome to the Note Investor Podcast. I'm your host, Dan Deppen, and today I'm going to be talking about how to read a report from a loan servicer. Uh, this is something a lot of new folks struggle with. I get a lot of questions about this. And while reading a report is fairly basic on one level, it can get a little bit challenging because no two servicers display data in the same way. And some of them use some really cryptic descriptions of their columns, and they just really don't make it easy for investors to figure out what's going on. So, per request, I'm going to go through some of this with you today. So, first of all, what is a servicer report, and what are we looking for? Well, there are a couple different kinds of reports you can generally pull out of a loan servicer's portal. So, when you buy a loan, you get it boarded with a servicer, they're always going to have some kind of portal that you log into that you can look at all the information on your loans. Most of the time, what we're looking for is a pay history report to see what payments have come in on the loan, how they've been allocated, how current the loan is, things like that. Um there's also a lot of other information. There's generally notes on the loan, um and sometimes call logs, where the loan servicer if they've made contact with the borrower either over the phone or through email, they'll document a lot of those things in there. Now, some servicers put really detailed notes on there. It makes it nice. Some of them are insanely cryptic. Um and are really impossible to decipher, and sometimes I have to email them to find out what on earth their notes meant. So, why are these things so important? Well, it tells you the performance of the loan, right? So, the pay history of the loan and the interactions the servicer has had with the borrower tell you is this a solid performing loan? Is a weekly performing loan? Is it a sub performer? Is it non performer? Is it really non performer? And so, we're going to refer to these reports continuously once you own a loan to keep track of your portfolio, and then they're also very important during the due diligence process when you're buying loans. So, before you even own the loan and you're considering making an offer, you've made an offer, and you're doing your due diligence to determine whether or not it's okay to close, you're always going to get a copy of the pay history report, and I always ask for the servicing notes from the seller cuz you can go through this. This is where you're really getting a going to get a good idea of the performance of the loan. Some of the other things we look for in these reports are they'll show line items for escrows. So, they'll show which portion of the payments were allocated escrows, the servicer will show if they've paid property taxes. Sometimes force placed insurance is handled through the loan servicer, it'll show that as well. So, there's a lot of really crucial information that you're going to pull out of these portals both when you're in that due diligence phase and then after you own the loan. So, today what I'll do is I'll go through just some of the basics of what you're looking for in these reports and things to understand. And also talk about some of the challenges. And and I think these the the the challenges will become apparent to you as I go through here. And basically those are as I already mentioned, no two servicers portals are remotely the same. You know, they like to make cryptic notes. And and sometimes you even end up running into differences between the data that's displayed or the format of the data that's displayed in the portal when you log in and then the format if you just say you do an export to a PDF file or an Excel, sometimes the way it the the numbers are the same but the way it's displayed can be different and that can cause additional confusion. So, some of the basics that we want to get right before we get started or in some of the main things we're looking for. So, on the report you'll see a number of rows and line items that could be payments that have come in from the borrower. Payments that may have gone out from the loan servicer, say for taxes or insurance. And in all of these it's going to show the actual date that that transaction occurred or the date paid. In addition to that, when the borrower makes payments, it's going to show a date due. And the date paid and the date due can sometimes be very, very different. So, for example, like let's say you see a payment on a loan and it came in October 1st, 2021, but the date due was March 1st, 2021. What that means what that's telling you is the borrower is behind on the loan, right? If the borrower was current, you know, let's say they had a payment due November 1st, you know, you would expect for that payment the date due to be November 1st, and then that date paid to be sometime in October, right? Assuming they're keeping up and paying on time. That's I'm guessing that's probably how you handle your mortgages and, you know, most of the people listening to this, but when you're buying non-performing loans, that's not the case. In some cases, the date due and the date paid can be a couple years apart. Um and so this is just a loan that's fallen behind. Um but but a lender's never foreclosed, or there could be a lot of reasons why there there could be a big gap between the date paid and the date due, but it's important to understand the difference between those two. Now, service report's also going to show the loan balance, which is obviously very, very important, and so you'll be able to look at all the rows, see how that balance has changed over time. Sometimes there are situations where depending on the terms of the loan and if the borrower is behind, I've had loans where the borrower was making payments, but the loan servicer was allocating all of those funds to interest, late fees, uh maybe lender advances, and actually none of it was going to principal. So, the other thing we'll look at is the breakdown for each payment that comes in, how the pieces of that payment were allocated. That's really important to understand because what you're ultimately going to do is enter that into your accounting system. I happen to use QuickBooks. So and in this podcast, I'm not going to really get into accounting cuz that's a whole subject into and of itself. But as you receive payments from borrowers, you need to track which portions of those payments go to principal, which payments are those or which portion of those payments go to interest because that's going to be very important when it comes time to doing your taxes. It's a column for loan balance. You can see that steadily dropping over time, which is what you want. That kind of implies the loan is probably current. Um So, the borrower is making payments and some of those portion of those payments are going to principal. And then, in the report, you'll see a few columns where they break out how each loan payment was applied. So, there should be one showing what was applied to principal, what was applied to interest. Um there's generally another one showing what was applied to escrows. Um sometimes they also say to impounds. Impounds, escrows, technically the the same thing. And then, sometimes they have something that's called reserve. So, what happens on occasion is, let's say a borrower makes extra payments. So, I've had borrowers pay ahead on loans. And if the borrower starts paying an extra amount, sometimes they pay an extra amount that's not a full payment. Like, let's say their payment is the P&I is $400 a month. And they randomly send in a $750 extra payment. Sometimes the loan servicer isn't sure how to apply that, so they can put it to they call it reserve and then reapply it to payments later. Um sometimes they call it to suspense, which means it's just like a holding thing until they allocate it later. Um there can also be a column showing any late fees that have been paid. So, loan to loan late fees can vary based on policies of the server and terms of the loan. Sometimes loans will specify specific loan fees or late fees. And then, it'll show a record type. Again, this is an area where servicers like to use super cryptic terminology and it can be a challenge to to figure out. So that So that was one from Madison. metadata.title: Mortgage Note Income Fund
metadata.author: 7e Investments
metadata.shortDescription:
10 years, six full-cycle funds, and more than 750 loans managed across 40+ states. In this walkthrough, 7e Investments CEO Chris Seveney explains how mortgage note investing steps into that situation, and how a negotiated payment plan can keep a borrower in their home while producing monthly income for investors.

This is a walkthrough of how the asset class works and how 7e runs the process, not a sales pitch. Chris covers:

* What a mortgage note is, and what it means to step into the lender’s seat
* How 7e buys non-performing first-position loans at a discount and works them back to reperforming
* The three Ps of underwriting: the property, the person, and the predicament
* How borrower equity and a discounted purchase basis act as two layers of capital protection
* The exit paths: selling a reperforming loan, a borrower payoff or refinance, or resolving through the property
* Why rising delinquencies and flat home values are increasing the supply of non-performing loans
* An overview of 7e’s Regulation A+ bond offering, open to accredited and non-accredited investors with a $5,000 minimum, and its Regulation D 506(c) Class E5 bond for verified accredited investors
* Reporting details: 1099-INT (no K-1), no UBIT for self-directed retirement accounts under current law, and audited financials filed with the SEC
* How to review the offering documents and take the next step

📞 Book a call with our team: https://link.oodapro.io/widget/booking/8oD6HuUffpmfVJ6bDc71
🌐 Review the offering documents: https://7einvestments.com
✉️ Email: invest@7einvestments.com
☎️ Phone: 866-226-5736

IMPORTANT DISCLOSURES: This video is for educational purposes only. It is not an offer to sell or a solicitation of an offer to buy any security. Any offer is made only through the applicable offering circular or private placement memorandum, available at 7einvestments.com. Regulation D 506(c) securities are available only to verified accredited investors. These investments are speculative and illiquid, involve substantial risk including possible loss of the entire investment, and returns and distributions are not guaranteed. Target rates depend on portfolio performance. Past performance does not guarantee future results. 
#MortgageNotes #NoteInvesting #PassiveIncome #RealEstateInvesting #NonPerformingLoans
